Chapter 10 — Sparsity and Feature Selection

Every penalty of the previous chapters shrank the weights but kept all of them: ridge regression, the support vector machine and the kernel methods use every feature, and only the support vectors, which are examples and not features, drop out. This chapter asks for something different: a model that uses only a few of the features, and that finds out by itself which ones. We start from the most direct formulation, choosing the best subset of features, and see why it is hard and why its training error is deceptive. We then follow two routes to a tractable method, greedy pursuit and the convex relaxation of the count of non-zero weights, which is the lasso; we derive its closed form in the simplest case, its optimality conditions and the algorithms that compute it (coordinate descent and proximal gradient, the relatives of the methods of Chapters 7 and 8). We measure what sparsity buys on real data, why correlated features make selection unstable (the elastic net), how the ideas carry over to classification, and, to close the loop opened in Chapters 2 and 5, why feature selection must be done inside the cross-validation loop.

10.1 Learning objectives¶

Chapter 4 showed that irrelevant features hurt a method based on distances, and Section 6.2.4 that nearly collinear features make the individual coefficients of least squares meaningless. Ridge regression handles both by shrinking, but it never says which features matter. Here we ask the model to say it.

After working through the chapter you will be able to:

  1. explain why a model that uses few features can be preferable (interpretation and cost, and also estimation error), and write the sparse learning problem with the count ∥w∥0\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0∥w∥0​ of non-zero weights;

  2. carry out best-subset selection exhaustively on a small problem, explain why the training error cannot choose the size of the subset, choose it with CpC_pCp​, BIC and cross-validation, and prove the covariance form of the optimism that shows why the effective degrees of freedom of a searched subset exceed its size;

  3. derive forward stepwise selection and orthogonal matching pursuit, and prove that the latter recovers the true support under the exact-recovery condition, and under a bound on the coherence of the features;

  4. define the lasso, derive soft-thresholding for an orthonormal design, prove the optimality conditions and the value of λ\lambdaλ above which the solution is zero, and read the penalty geometrically (the corners of the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ ball) and as a Laplace prior;

  5. derive and implement coordinate descent and proximal gradient (ISTA and FISTA) for the lasso, prove the O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) rate of the latter, and show on data why the plain subgradient method is a poor choice;

  6. choose λ\lambdaλ by cross-validation with the one-standard-error rule, interpret the number of non-zero coefficients as the degrees of freedom of the lasso, and prove the slow-rate bound that shows why the number of useless features enters the error only through its logarithm;

  7. explain why the lasso selects arbitrarily among correlated features, define the elastic net, and prove the grouping effect;

  8. fit an ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​-penalized logistic regression, see that the representer theorem of Chapter 9 fails for the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ penalty, and perform feature selection inside the cross-validation loop, measuring the leak of selecting outside it and the invalid ppp-values that follow a selection.

Prerequisites. Chapters 1 to 9. In particular the leakage and the pipelines of Section 2.7, the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ and ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ Rademacher complexities of Section 3.8 and Exercise 3.9, the irrelevant features of Section 4.7.2, the one-standard-error rule (Section 5.4.1) and nested cross-validation (Section 5.4.3), collinearity and VIF (Section 6.2.4), the optimism of ridge (Proposition 6.5) and the three views of the penalty (Section 6.3.5), regularized logistic regression (Section 6.5), the descent lemma and Nesterov’s acceleration (Proposition 7.2 and Theorem 7.9), and the subgradient and dual coordinate methods of Section 8.5.

A word about the data in this chapter

The experiments use real data sets shipped with scikit-learn: Diabetes (the 331/111 split of Chapters 6, 7 and 9, features standardized with the training statistics), Breast Cancer (the stratified 426/143 split of Chapters 6, 8 and 9, malignant =1=1=1) and Digits (only the digits 3 and 8 in Sections 10.9 and 10.11). Four kinds of experiment are not plain data, and are flagged where they occur: (i) real features with appended noise columns, as in Section 4.7.2; (ii) a Gaussian design for the support-recovery experiment of Section 10.4, where the true support must be known; (iii) a simulated world on the real Diabetes design, with the least-squares fit as the truth, as in Section 6.3.3, to verify a formula for the degrees of freedom; (iv) shuffled labels on real features, a world in which by construction no feature carries any information about the label. The test patients of Diabetes are used once, in Section 10.7.3.

10.2 Why a model with few features?¶

10.2.1 Three reasons¶

Interpretation and cost. A model with five features can be read, audited and explained to the person whose data it uses; a model with five hundred cannot. Every feature also has a price in deployment: a laboratory test to order, a sensor to maintain, a column to keep clean. If a handful of features give the same accuracy, the rest are a liability.

Estimation error. The second reason is statistical and does not depend on taste. By Theorem 6.1, least squares on ppp features has an excess prediction error of σ2p/n\sigma^2p/nσ2p/n on the training inputs whatever the truth is: every feature that we estimate costs σ2/n\sigma^2/nσ2/n, including the ones whose true weight is zero. If the response depends on only s≪ps\ll ps≪p of the features, and someone told us which, the same estimator would cost σ2s/n\sigma^2s/nσ2s/n. The gap σ2(p−s)/n\sigma^2(p-s)/nσ2(p−s)/n is the price of the useless features; Section 4.7.2 measured it for the nearest neighbors, and we shall measure it for linear models in Section 10.7.4.

The price of not being told. We are not told which features matter, and looking for them costs something too. The theory of the problem (Donoho and Johnstone, 1994, in the further reading) says that the unavoidable price of not knowing the support is a factor of order ln⁡p\ln plnp on top of the σ2s/n\sigma^2s/nσ2s/n of the oracle: the error of the best possible procedure is of order σ2 sln⁡(p/s)/n\sigma^2\,s\ln(p/s)/nσ2sln(p/s)/n. Selection is therefore worth doing when sln⁡p≪ps\ln p\ll pslnp≪p, that is, when the true model is much smaller than the number of candidates, and the whole chapter can be read as the study of procedures that pay no more than this price.

10.2.2 Counting the non-zero weights¶

The number of features that a linear model uses is the number of non-zero entries of the weight vector.

Definition 10.1 (sparsity)

For w∈Rp\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^pw∈Rp let ∥w∥0=#{j:wj≠0}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0 = \#\{j: w_j\neq 0\}∥w∥0​=#{j:wj​=0} be the number of non-zero coordinates, and supp⁡(w)={j:wj≠0}\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf{w}) = \{j: w_j\ne 0\}supp(w)={j:wj​=0} the support. The vector is sss-sparse if ∥w∥0≤s\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0\le s∥w∥0​≤s. The best-subset problem with budget sss is

min⁡w∈Rp 12∥y−Xw∥2subject to∥w∥0≤s,(10.1)\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^p}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0\le s, \tag{10.1}w∈Rpmin​ 21​∥y−Xw∥2subject to∥w∥0​≤s,(10.1)
(1)

and its penalized form minimizes 12∥y−Xw∥2+λ0∥w∥0\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + \lambda_0\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_021​∥y−Xw∥2+λ0​∥w∥0​.

The “ℓ0\ell_0ℓ0​ norm” is not a norm: ∥cw∥0=∥w∥0\lVert c\mathbf{w}\rVert_0 = \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0∥cw∥0​=∥w∥0​ for every c≠0c\neq 0c=0, so it is not homogeneous, and the set {∥w∥0≤s}\{\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0\le s\}{∥w∥0​≤s} is a union of (ps)\binom{p}{s}(sp​) coordinate subspaces, not a convex set. For a fixed support SSS the problem is ordinary least squares on the columns in SSS, so (10.1) is solved by trying all the supports. The next cell counts them, and shows how quickly this stops being possible.

def human_time(seconds):
    for unit, size in [("years", 3600 * 24 * 365), ("days", 3600 * 24), ("hours", 3600), ("minutes", 60)]:
        if seconds >= size:
            return f"{seconds / size:.3g} {unit}"
    return f"{seconds:.2g} s"


rows = []
for p_, s_ in [(10, 3), (10, 10), (30, 5), (30, 10), (100, 5), (100, 10), (1000, 5)]:
    count = comb(p_, s_)
    rows.append({"p": p_, "s": s_, "supports of size s": f"{count:.3g}", "time at 10^6 fits/s": human_time(count / 1e6)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

For p=10p = 10p=10 the search is instantaneous; for p=30p = 30p=30 and s=10s = 10s=10 it is already 3×1073\times10^73×107 fits; for p=100p = 100p=100 and s=10s = 10s=10 it is far beyond reach. The general problem is NP-hard (Natarajan, 1995), and although specialized branch-and-bound algorithms solve problems with a few hundred features, no polynomial algorithm is known or expected. The rest of the chapter is about what to do instead; but first we use the small problem that we can solve exactly, to see what the exact answer looks like and what its weak points are.

10.3 Best-subset selection¶

10.3.1 The exhaustive search on Diabetes¶

The Diabetes data of Chapters 6, 7 and 9 have p=10p = 10p=10 features, so there are 210−1=10232^{10}-1 = 1023210−1=1023 non-empty subsets. We use the same split of Chapter 6 (331 training and 111 test patients) and standardize the features with the training statistics, as in Chapter 7. With centered columns and a centered target the intercept is the mean of the target, and the fit of a subset SSS is the least-squares fit on the columns in SSS. For each subset we compute the residual sum of squares RSS(S)\mathrm{RSS}(S)RSS(S).

diab = load_diabetes()
feat = list(diab.feature_names)
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(diab.data, diab.target, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED)
scaler_d = StandardScaler().fit(Xd_tr)
Zd, Zd_te = scaler_d.transform(Xd_tr), scaler_d.transform(Xd_te)
n_d, p_d = Zd.shape
yc = yd_tr - yd_tr.mean()                     # centered target: the intercept is the training mean
print(f"training patients {n_d}, test patients {len(yd_te)}, features {p_d}: {feat}")


def rss_of(S, Z, y):
    """Residual sum of squares of least squares on the columns S of Z (empty S: the null model)."""
    if len(S) == 0:
        return float(y @ y)
    A = Z[:, list(S)]
    b = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0]
    r = y - A @ b
    return float(r @ r)


subsets = [S for k in range(1, p_d + 1) for S in itertools.combinations(range(p_d), k)]
size_all = np.array([len(S) for S in subsets])
t0 = time.time()
rss_all = np.array([rss_of(S, Zd, yc) for S in subsets])
print(f"{len(subsets)} subsets searched in {time.time() - t0:.2f} s (this machine; the point is that it is instantaneous)")

# Best subset of each size, and the criteria of the next subsection.
rss_null = float(yc @ yc)
rss_full = rss_all[-1]
sigma2_hat = rss_full / (n_d - p_d - 1)        # unbiased estimate of sigma^2 from the full model (Theorem 6.1)
best_S = {0: ()}
best_rss = {0: rss_null}
for k in range(1, p_d + 1):
    idx = np.where(size_all == k)[0]
    j = idx[np.argmin(rss_all[idx])]
    best_S[k], best_rss[k] = subsets[j], rss_all[j]
cp = {k: best_rss[k] / n_d + 2 * sigma2_hat * (k + 1) / n_d for k in best_S}
bic = {k: n_d * np.log(best_rss[k] / n_d) + np.log(n_d) * (k + 1) for k in best_S}
table = pd.DataFrame({
    "size": list(best_S),
    "best subset": [", ".join(feat[j] for j in best_S[k]) or "(none)" for k in best_S],
    "training MSE": [best_rss[k] / n_d for k in best_S],
    "C_p": [cp[k] for k in best_S],
    "BIC": [bic[k] for k in best_S],
})
print(table.round(1).to_string(index=False))
print(f"sigma^2 hat = {sigma2_hat:.0f} (sigma hat = {np.sqrt(sigma2_hat):.1f}, Chapter 6: 54.15 on all 442 patients)")

Three things can be read in the table. First, the training MSE falls steeply at the start, from 6,044.66{,}044.66,044.6 for the null model to 3,931.03{,}931.03,931.0 with the body mass index alone and 3,387.13{,}387.13,387.1 with the index and s5, and then very slowly, to 2,907.32{,}907.32,907.3 with all ten features: going from six to ten features reduces it by less than 1%1\%1%. Second, the best subsets are not nested. The best subset of size 5 contains s3, but the best subset of size 6 drops it and adds s1 and s2 instead: these two features are strongly correlated (the correlation of the standardized training columns is 0.89, Section 6.2.4), and each is useful mostly in the presence of the other. A procedure that adds one feature at a time cannot reach such a subset, as we shall see in Section 10.3.3. Third, the two criteria agree that the interesting range is 5 to 7 features and differ by one in the minimum: CpC_pCp​ is smallest at size 7 (3,060.83{,}060.83,060.8, against 3,061.53{,}061.53,061.5 at size 6) and the BIC at size 6 (2,683.42{,}683.42,683.4, against 2,683.82{,}683.82,683.8 at size 5), so sizes 5, 6 and 7 are practically tied and the location of the minimum is not a sharp statement.

Proposition 10.1 (the training error cannot choose the size). Let RSSk∗\mathrm{RSS}^*_kRSSk∗​ be the smallest residual sum of squares over the subsets of size kkk. Then RSSk+1∗≤RSSk∗\mathrm{RSS}^*_{k+1}\le \mathrm{RSS}^*_kRSSk+1∗​≤RSSk∗​ for every kkk.

Proof. Let SSS be a subset of size kkk that attains RSSk∗\mathrm{RSS}^*_kRSSk∗​, and j∉Sj\notin Sj∈/S any other feature. The least-squares fit on S∪{j}S\cup\{j\}S∪{j} minimizes over a larger set of weight vectors than the fit on SSS (it contains all those with wj=0w_j = 0wj​=0), so RSS(S∪{j})≤RSS(S)\mathrm{RSS}(S\cup\{j\})\le\mathrm{RSS}(S)RSS(S∪{j})≤RSS(S). The best subset of size k+1k+1k+1 can only do better. □\square□

The training error is therefore minimized by the largest subset, exactly as the training error of kkk-NN is minimized by k=1k=1k=1 (Section 4.3.2): it measures the fit to the data used in the choice, and the choice always favors more flexibility. Figure 10.1(a) shows all the 1023 subsets, and the best of each size.

10.3.2 Choosing the size: CpC_pCp​, BIC and cross-validation¶

To choose the size we need an estimate of the test error of the model of each size, which is the training error plus the optimism (Section 3.4). For ridge regression Proposition 6.5 expressed the optimism through the trace of the smoother. The following identity is the general form, and does not need the estimator to be linear. Let the training inputs be fixed, yi=μi+εiy_i = \mu_i + \varepsilon_iyi​=μi​+εi​ with independent errors of mean zero and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, let y^i\hat y_iy^​i​ be any estimator computed from the vector y\mathbf{y}y, and let yi∗=μi+εi∗y_i^\ast = \mu_i + \varepsilon_i^\astyi∗​=μi​+εi∗​ be new responses at the same inputs, with errors independent of the first.

an estimate of the expected test error at the training inputs. With Gaussian errors the AIC is equivalent up to constants, and the BIC of Schwarz replaces the factor 2 in the penalty by ln⁡n\ln nlnn (we use nln⁡(RSS/n)+(ln⁡n)(∣S∣+1)n\ln(\mathrm{RSS}/n) + (\ln n)(\lvert S\rvert+1)nln(RSS/n)+(lnn)(∣S∣+1)): it penalizes more heavily when n>e2≈7.4n > e^2\approx 7.4n>e2≈7.4, and it is consistent for the true support under conditions (it selects the right subset with probability tending to one), while CpC_pCp​ and AIC tend to select too many features. Both are computed in the table above.

There is a catch, and it is the central point of this subsection. The covariance formula holds for any estimator, and the estimator “the best subset of size kkk” is not least squares on a fixed set: it looks at y\mathbf{y}y to choose the set. Its degrees of freedom are not k+1k+1k+1, because y^i\hat y_iy^​i​ depends on yiy_iyi​ also through the choice of the features. We can measure it in a world where the answer is known. Take the real design and shuffle the labels: the features then carry no information about the response (μi\mu_iμi​ is constant), and for the centered response the covariance reduces to E[y⊤y^]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}^\top\hat{\mathbf{y}}]E[y⊤y^​], which is the expected reduction of the residual sum of squares. For a fixed subset of size kkk the expected reduction is kσ2k\sigma^2kσ2, that is, kkk degrees of freedom. For the best of the (10k)\binom{10}{k}(k10​) subsets it is larger.

def df_best_subset(Z, yc_, sizes, n_perm=500, seed=SEED):
    """Monte Carlo degrees of freedom of 'best subset of size k' in the null world (shuffled responses).
    df = E[reduction of the RSS] / sigma^2 with sigma^2 = ||y||^2/(n-1); a fixed subset of size k has df = k."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = len(yc_)
    s2 = float(yc_ @ yc_) / (n - 1)
    G = Z.T @ Z
    out = {}
    for k in sizes:
        idx = np.array([S for S in itertools.combinations(range(Z.shape[1]), k)])          # (m, k)
        Ginv = np.linalg.inv(G[idx[:, :, None], idx[:, None, :]])                          # (m, k, k)
        reductions = np.empty(n_perm)
        for r in range(n_perm):
            c = Z.T @ rng.permutation(yc_)                                                 # (p,)
            cs = c[idx]                                                                    # (m, k)
            reductions[r] = np.einsum("mi,mij,mj->m", cs, Ginv, cs).max()
        out[k] = (reductions.mean() / s2, reductions.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_perm) / s2)
    return out


df_null = df_best_subset(Zd, yc, [1, 2, 3, 5, 10])
df_table = pd.DataFrame({"size k": list(df_null),
                         "subsets searched": [comb(p_d, k) for k in df_null],
                         "df of a fixed subset": list(df_null),
                         "df of the best subset": [v[0] for v in df_null.values()],
                         "Monte Carlo SE": [v[1] for v in df_null.values()]})
print(df_table.round(2).to_string(index=False))

      5               252                     5                   8.71            0.17

The single best feature among ten has not one but about 3.4 degrees of freedom (Monte Carlo standard error 0.1), the best pair among 45 has 5.5, the best triple among 120 has 7.1 and the best five among 252 have 8.7; only for k=10k = 10k=10, where there is nothing to choose, does the count return to the size of the model (the table gives 10.2, within about one standard error of 10). Searching is paid for in degrees of freedom: the procedure “take the best of the ten features” fits the noise like a model with 3.4 free parameters, so that a criterion that charges it for one will underestimate its optimism by a factor of three. (This is the null world, where the choice is purely random; with a strong signal the choice is more stable and the inflation smaller, as Ye (1998) showed.) The effect is the winner’s curse of Sections 3.4.1 and 5.2.3 in another form, and it grows with the number of candidates: it is the reason why CpC_pCp​ and the BIC, computed with df=k+1\mathrm{df} = k+1df=k+1, favor models chosen from many candidates.

The remedy is not to correct the formula but to estimate the error of the whole procedure, including the search, by cross-validation: in each fold the search is repeated on the training part, and the chosen model is evaluated on the validation part. The standardization is also repeated in each fold (Section 2.7). This is the only estimate of Section 10.3 that accounts for the fact that the subset was chosen by looking at the data.

def cv_best_subset(X, y, n_folds=10, seed=SEED):
    """Cross-validated MSE of 'best subset of size k' for k = 0..p, repeating the standardization and the whole search in each fold."""
    kf = KFold(n_folds, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    errs = np.zeros((n_folds, X.shape[1] + 1))
    for f, (tr, va) in enumerate(kf.split(X)):
        sc = StandardScaler().fit(X[tr])
        A, B = sc.transform(X[tr]), sc.transform(X[va])
        ym = y[tr].mean()
        yt = y[tr] - ym
        rss_f = np.array([rss_of(S, A, yt) for S in subsets])
        errs[f, 0] = np.mean((y[va] - ym) ** 2)
        for k in range(1, X.shape[1] + 1):
            idx = np.where(size_all == k)[0]
            S = list(subsets[idx[np.argmin(rss_f[idx])]])
            b = np.linalg.lstsq(A[:, S], yt, rcond=None)[0]
            errs[f, k] = np.mean((y[va] - ym - B[:, S] @ b) ** 2)
    return errs


cv_errs = cv_best_subset(Xd_tr, yd_tr)

Panel (a) of Figure 10.1 shows how much the choice of the subset matters: with five features the training MSE ranges from 2,9902{,}9902,990 (the best subset) to about 5,1005{,}1005,100 (the worst) according to which five. Panel (b) compares the three estimates of the error. The cross-validation curve, which repeats the whole search in every fold, drops sharply up to two features and is flat from five to ten: its values (3,2183{,}2183,218 at 5, 3,1183{,}1183,118 at 7, 3,1433{,}1433,143 at 10) differ by far less than the standard error of each (about 200). The minimum is at 7 features, the one-standard-error rule (Section 5.4.1) chooses the smallest model within one standard error of it, 5 features (sex, bmi, bp, s3, s5), and CpC_pCp​ and the BIC choose 7 and 6. All four choices lie between 5 and 7 features, which is the honest summary: on these 331 patients the data say “between five and seven features”, not a specific number. The vertical gap between the training MSE and the cross-validated error at ten features is 236, close to the optimism 2σ^2(p+1)/n=2002\hat\sigma^2(p+1)/n = 2002σ^2(p+1)/n=200 that Proposition 10.2 predicts for a fixed model with 11 parameters (the cross-validation estimate is slightly pessimistic because each fold trains on 90% of the data).

10.3.3 Greedy search: forward and backward stepwise selection¶

When ppp is too large for the exhaustive search we can build the subset one feature at a time. Forward stepwise selection starts from the empty model and, at each step, adds the feature whose inclusion reduces the residual sum of squares the most; backward elimination starts from the full model and removes, at each step, the feature whose removal increases it the least. Forward selection needs p+(p−1)+…p + (p-1) + \dotsp+(p−1)+… fits, a number quadratic in ppp instead of 2p2^p2p. The next lemma shows that each step is cheap: no refit is needed to rank the candidates.

Lemma 10.3 (the gain of adding a feature). Let rS=y−PSy\mathbf{r}_S = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{P}_S\mathbf{y}rS​=y−PS​y be the residual of the least-squares fit on the columns SSS, and let j∉Sj\notin Sj∈/S with x~j=(I−PS)xj≠0\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_S)\mathbf{x}_j\neq\mathbf{0}x~j​=(I−PS​)xj​=0 the part of xj\mathbf{x}_jxj​ orthogonal to the columns in SSS. Then

RSS(S)−RSS(S∪{j})=(xj⊤rS)2∥x~j∥2.\mathrm{RSS}(S) - \mathrm{RSS}(S\cup\{j\}) = \frac{(\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}_S)^2}{\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j\rVert^2}.RSS(S)−RSS(S∪{j})=∥x~j​∥2(xj⊤​rS​)2​.
(4)
Proof

The span of S∪{j}S\cup\{j\}S∪{j} is the orthogonal sum of the span of SSS and the line through x~j\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_jx~j​, so PS∪{j}y=PSy+x~jx~j⊤y/∥x~j∥2\mathbf{P}_{S\cup\{j\}}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{P}_S\mathbf{y} + \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j^\top\mathbf{y}/\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j\rVert^2PS∪{j}​y=PS​y+x~j​x~j⊤​y/∥x~j​∥2, and the residual sum of squares falls by the squared length of the second term, (x~j⊤y)2/∥x~j∥2(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j^\top\mathbf{y})^2/\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j\rVert^2(x~j⊤​y)2/∥x~j​∥2. Finally x~j⊤y=xj⊤(I−PS)y=xj⊤rS\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j^\top\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}_j^\top(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_S)\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}_Sx~j⊤​y=xj⊤​(I−PS​)y=xj⊤​rS​, since I−PS\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_SI−PS​ is a symmetric projection. □\square□

The numerator is the correlation of the candidate with the current residual, and the denominator discounts a candidate that is almost in the span of the features already chosen. Forward selection is greedy: it never reconsiders a choice, and it can miss the best subset, because the usefulness of a feature depends on the others (Exercise 3.6 had a first example). We compare it with the exhaustive answer.

def forward_selection(Z, y, k_max=None):
    """Forward stepwise selection: returns the features in the order in which they enter (Lemma 10.3)."""
    n, p = Z.shape
    k_max = k_max or p
    S, r = [], y.copy()
    for _ in range(k_max):
        best_j, best_gain = None, -1.0
        for j in range(p):
            if j in S:
                continue
            if S:
                P = Z[:, S] @ np.linalg.pinv(Z[:, S])
                xt = Z[:, j] - P @ Z[:, j]
            else:
                xt = Z[:, j]
            nrm = float(xt @ xt)
            if nrm < 1e-12:
                continue
            gain = float(Z[:, j] @ r) ** 2 / nrm
            if gain > best_gain:
                best_j, best_gain = j, gain
        S.append(best_j)
        b = np.linalg.lstsq(Z[:, S], y, rcond=None)[0]
        r = y - Z[:, S] @ b
    return S


order_fwd = forward_selection(Zd, yc)

for k in range(1, p_d + 1):

Forward selection finds the best subset for sizes 1 to 5 and for sizes 9 and 10, and misses it for sizes 6, 7 and 8: the best subsets there require removing s3, which entered at step 4, and adding the correlated pair s1 and s2. The loss is small. At size 6 the forward subset has a training MSE of 2,945.32{,}945.32,945.3 against 2,934.32{,}934.32,934.3 for the best (0.4%0.4\%0.4% more), and at size 7 2,931.22{,}931.22,931.2 against 2,915.52{,}915.52,915.5 (0.5%0.5\%0.5%). Greedy search is a good approximation when the features are not too correlated and the main practical choice when ppp is large; with correlated features it can commit early to a feature that a pair will later make redundant. (Backward elimination starts from the full model and therefore needs p<np<np<n.) The criterion of Lemma 10.3 has a cheaper relative, which is the subject of the next section: rank the candidates by their correlation with the residual only.

10.4 Orthogonal matching pursuit¶

10.4.1 The algorithm¶

Forward selection ranks the candidates by the gain of Lemma 10.3. Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP), a method from signal processing (Pati, Rezaiifar and Krishnaprasad, 1993; Tropp, 2004), ranks them by the simpler quantity ∣xj⊤r∣\lvert\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}\rvert∣xj⊤​r∣, the correlation of the feature with the current residual, without dividing by ∥x~j∥\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j\rVert∥x~j​∥. After each choice the coefficients of all the selected features are refitted by least squares (this is the “orthogonal” part: the residual is always orthogonal to the selected columns).

Algorithm (orthogonal matching pursuit)

Start with S=∅S = \varnothingS=∅ and r=y\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y}r=y. Repeat sss times:

  1. choose j∗=arg⁡max⁡j∉S∣xj⊤r∣j^\ast = \arg\max_{j\notin S}\lvert\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}\rvertj∗=argmaxj∈/S​∣xj⊤​r∣ and set S←S∪{j∗}S\leftarrow S\cup\{j^\ast\}S←S∪{j∗};

  2. fit least squares on the columns in SSS and set r=y−PSy\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{P}_S\mathbf{y}r=y−PS​y. Return SSS and the least-squares coefficients on SSS.

For columns with the same norm and nearly orthogonal to each other the two rules coincide, since then ∥x~j∥≈∥xj∥\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j\rVert\approx\lVert\mathbf{x}_j\rVert∥x~j​∥≈∥xj​∥; they differ when a candidate is almost explained by the selected features, which forward selection discounts and OMP does not. The cost of a step is one product X⊤r\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{r}X⊤r and a small least-squares problem, so OMP is the cheapest of the selection methods, and it is the method for which the cleanest guarantees exist.

def omp(Z, y, s):
    """Orthogonal matching pursuit: indices in order of entry and the least-squares coefficients on them."""
    S, r = [], y.copy()
    for _ in range(s):
        c = np.abs(Z.T @ r)
        c[S] = -1.0
        S.append(int(np.argmax(c)))
        b = np.linalg.lstsq(Z[:, S], y, rcond=None)[0]
        r = y - Z[:, S] @ b
    return S, b


order_omp, _ = omp(Zd, yc, p_d)
sk = OrthogonalMatchingPursuit(n_nonzero_coefs=4, fit_intercept=False).fit(Zd, yc)
print("OMP order      :", [feat[j] for j in order_omp])
print("forward order  :", [feat[j] for j in order_fwd])
print("first four, ours vs scikit-learn:", sorted(order_omp[:4]) == sorted(np.flatnonzero(sk.coef_)))
OMP order      : ['bmi', 's5', 'bp', 's3', 'sex', 's2', 'age', 's6', 's4', 's1']
forward order  : ['bmi', 's5', 'bp', 's3', 'sex', 's1', 's4', 's2', 'age', 's6']
first four, ours vs scikit-learn: True

The three methods enter the same five features in the same order (bmi, s5, bp, s3, sex), and the first four are the best subset of size 4 found by the exhaustive search; they differ at the sixth step, where forward selection adds s1 (the feature whose gain is the largest once the others are in) and OMP adds s2 (the one most correlated with the residual). OMP leaves s1 for the very last step, because it is almost a combination of s2 and the other features (the correlation of the two is 0.89), and our implementation agrees with the one in scikit-learn.

10.4.2 When does it find the true features?¶

Suppose that the truth is y=XS∗w∗\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}\mathbf{w}^\asty=XS∗​w∗ with ∣S∗∣=s\lvert S^\ast\rvert = s∣S∗∣=s and no noise. When does OMP select the features of S∗S^\astS∗, and nothing else, in sss steps? The answer depends on how well the wrong features can be mimicked by the right ones. We assume that the columns have unit norm, ∥xj∥=1\lVert\mathbf{x}_j\rVert = 1∥xj​∥=1, and that the columns in S∗S^\astS∗ are linearly independent. Let XS+=(XS⊤XS)−1XS⊤\mathbf{X}_S^+ = (\mathbf{X}_S^\top\mathbf{X}_S)^{-1}\mathbf{X}_S^\topXS+​=(XS⊤​XS​)−1XS⊤​ be the pseudo-inverse of the columns in SSS.

Theorem 10.4 (exact recovery by OMP, noiseless case)

If

max⁡j∉S∗ ∥XS∗+xj∥1<1(10.3)\max_{j\notin S^\ast}\ \lVert\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^+\mathbf{x}_j\rVert_1 < 1 \tag{10.3}j∈/S∗max​ ∥XS∗+​xj​∥1​<1(10.3)
(5)

(the exact recovery condition, ERC), then OMP selects only features of S∗S^\astS∗ and, after sss steps, returns exactly S∗S^\astS∗ and w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗, for every w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ supported on S∗S^\astS∗.

The quantity in (10.3) is the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm of the coefficients of the regression of the wrong feature xj\mathbf{x}_jxj​ on the right ones. If it is below one, no wrong feature can be built from the right ones with enough weight to look better than the right ones.

Proof

Suppose that at some step OMP has selected a subset T⊂S∗T\subset S^\astT⊂S∗ (true at the beginning, when T=∅T=\varnothingT=∅), with T≠S∗T\neq S^\astT=S∗. The residual is r=(I−PT)XS∗w∗\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_T)\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}\mathbf{w}^\astr=(I−PT​)XS∗​w∗, which is the projection of a vector of span⁡(XS∗)\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast})span(XS∗​) on a subspace of it, so r∈span⁡(XS∗)\mathbf{r}\in\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast})r∈span(XS∗​), and r≠0\mathbf{r}\neq\mathbf{0}r=0 because the columns of S∗S^\astS∗ are independent and some coefficient of S∗∖TS^\ast\setminus TS∗∖T is non-zero (if some of them are zero, replace S∗S^\astS∗ by the support of w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ in the argument). Since r\mathbf{r}r is in the span of XS∗\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}XS∗​ we can write r=XS∗(XS∗⊤XS∗)−1XS∗⊤r\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}(\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^\top\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast})^{-1}\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^\top\mathbf{r}r=XS∗​(XS∗⊤​XS∗​)−1XS∗⊤​r, and for any j∉S∗j\notin S^\astj∈/S∗

xj⊤r=(XS∗+xj)⊤(XS∗⊤r),so∣xj⊤r∣≤∥XS∗+xj∥1 ∥XS∗⊤r∥∞<∥XS∗⊤r∥∞=max⁡i∈S∗∣xi⊤r∣,\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r} = \big(\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^+\mathbf{x}_j\big)^\top\big(\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^\top\mathbf{r}\big),\qquad\text{so}\qquad\lvert\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}\rvert\le\lVert\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^+\mathbf{x}_j\rVert_1\,\lVert\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^\top\mathbf{r}\rVert_\infty < \lVert\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^\top\mathbf{r}\rVert_\infty = \max_{i\in S^\ast}\lvert\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{r}\rvert,xj⊤​r=(XS∗+​xj​)⊤(XS∗⊤​r),so∣xj⊤​r∣≤∥XS∗+​xj​∥1​∥XS∗⊤​r∥∞​<∥XS∗⊤​r∥∞​=i∈S∗max​∣xi⊤​r∣,
(6)

using Hölder’s inequality and (10.3); the strict inequality holds because ∥XS∗⊤r∥∞>0\lVert\mathbf{X}_{S^\ast}^\top\mathbf{r}\rVert_\infty > 0∥XS∗⊤​r∥∞​>0 (otherwise r\mathbf{r}r would be orthogonal to its own span, hence zero). The maximum on the right is attained at some i∈S∗i\in S^\asti∈S∗, and i∉Ti\notin Ti∈/T because the residual is orthogonal to the selected columns, so xi⊤r=0\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{r} = 0xi⊤​r=0 for i∈Ti\in Ti∈T. Hence the best candidate is a true feature not yet selected. By induction, after sss steps T=S∗T = S^\astT=S∗, and least squares on S∗S^\astS∗ recovers w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ exactly because the data are noiseless. □\square□

The condition (10.3) involves S∗S^\astS∗, which we do not know. A condition on the data alone, valid for every S∗S^\astS∗ of a given size, is obtained from the mutual coherence μ=max⁡i≠j∣xi⊤xj∣\mu = \max_{i\ne j}\lvert\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j\rvertμ=maxi=j​∣xi⊤​xj​∣ of the unit-norm columns.

Corollary 10.5. If μ(2s−1)<1\mu(2s-1) < 1μ(2s−1)<1, then the ERC holds for every support of size sss, and OMP recovers every sss-sparse noiseless signal.

Proof

Let G=XS⊤XS=I+E\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{X}_{S}^\top\mathbf{X}_{S} = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{E}G=XS⊤​XS​=I+E with ∣S∣=s\lvert S\rvert = s∣S∣=s. The off-diagonal entries of E\mathbf{E}E are at most μ\muμ in absolute value, so every column of E\mathbf{E}E has ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm at most (s−1)μ<1(s-1)\mu<1(s−1)μ<1, and the Neumann series gives ∥G−1∥1→1≤1/(1−(s−1)μ)\lVert\mathbf{G}^{-1}\rVert_{1\to1}\le 1/(1-(s-1)\mu)∥G−1∥1→1​≤1/(1−(s−1)μ), where ∥⋅∥1→1\lVert\cdot\rVert_{1\to1}∥⋅∥1→1​ is the largest absolute column sum, the operator norm for the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm. For j∉Sj\notin Sj∈/S the vector XS⊤xj\mathbf{X}_S^\top\mathbf{x}_jXS⊤​xj​ has sss entries of absolute value at most μ\muμ, so ∥XS⊤xj∥1≤sμ\lVert\mathbf{X}_S^\top\mathbf{x}_j\rVert_1\le s\mu∥XS⊤​xj​∥1​≤sμ. Therefore ∥XS+xj∥1=∥G−1XS⊤xj∥1≤sμ/(1−(s−1)μ)\lVert\mathbf{X}_S^+\mathbf{x}_j\rVert_1 = \lVert\mathbf{G}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_S^\top\mathbf{x}_j\rVert_1\le s\mu/(1-(s-1)\mu)∥XS+​xj​∥1​=∥G−1XS⊤​xj​∥1​≤sμ/(1−(s−1)μ), which is below one if and only if sμ<1−(s−1)μs\mu < 1-(s-1)\musμ<1−(s−1)μ, that is, (2s−1)μ<1(2s-1)\mu<1(2s−1)μ<1. □\square□

The corollary says that OMP can recover sss features if the features are nearly orthogonal, in the sense that μ<1/(2s−1)\mu<1/(2s-1)μ<1/(2s−1). For s=5s = 5s=5 this needs μ<1/9\mu<1/9μ<1/9, and for random unit vectors in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn the coherence is of order 2ln⁡p/n\sqrt{2\ln p/n}2lnp/n​, so the condition holds when n≳s2ln⁡pn\gtrsim s^2\ln pn≳s2lnp. That is conservative: the experiment below shows that nnn of order sln⁡ps\ln pslnp is enough in practice. On real data the condition is hopeless, because real features are correlated:

Gram = Zd.T @ Zd / n_d
np.fill_diagonal(Gram, 0.0)
mu_coh = np.abs(Gram).max()
i_, j_ = np.unravel_index(np.abs(Gram).argmax(), Gram.shape)
print(f"coherence of the 10 standardized Diabetes features: {mu_coh:.3f} (features {feat[i_]} and {feat[j_]})")
print(f"Corollary 10.5 would need mu < 1/(2s-1): s = 1 -> {1:.0f}, s = 2 -> {1/3:.2f}, s = 3 -> {1/5:.2f}")


def erc_value(Z, S):
    """The left-hand side of (10.3) for the support S (columns normalized to unit norm)."""
    U = Z / np.linalg.norm(Z, axis=0)
    P = np.linalg.pinv(U[:, list(S)])
    return max(np.abs(P @ U[:, j]).sum() for j in range(U.shape[1]) if j not in S)


print("ERC value for S = {bmi}      :", round(erc_value(Zd, [feat.index("bmi")]), 3))
print("ERC value for S = {bmi, s5}  :", round(erc_value(Zd, [feat.index("bmi"), feat.index("s5")]), 3))
print("ERC value for S = {bmi, bp, s3, s5}:", round(erc_value(Zd, [feat.index(f) for f in ["bmi", "bp", "s3", "s5"]]), 3))
coherence of the 10 standardized Diabetes features: 0.893 (features s1 and s2)
Corollary 10.5 would need mu < 1/(2s-1): s = 1 -> 1, s = 2 -> 0.33, s = 3 -> 0.20
ERC value for S = {bmi}      : 0.451
ERC value for S = {bmi, s5}  : 0.72
ERC value for S = {bmi, bp, s3, s5}: 1.02

The coherence of the Diabetes features is 0.893 (the pair s1, s2), so Corollary 10.5 gives a guarantee only for s=1s=1s=1 (it needs μ<1\mu<1μ<1) and none for s≥2s\ge 2s≥2 (it needs μ<1/3\mu<1/3μ<1/3, 1/51/51/5, ...). The exact recovery condition (10.3), computed for particular supports, is more informative: it holds for S∗={bmi}S^\ast=\{\texttt{bmi}\}S∗={bmi} (0.45) and for S∗={bmi,s5}S^\ast=\{\texttt{bmi},\texttt{s5}\}S∗={bmi,s5} (0.72), and just fails for the four-feature support {bmi,bp,s3,s5}\{\texttt{bmi},\texttt{bp},\texttt{s3},\texttt{s5}\}{bmi,bp,s3,s5} (1.02): the remaining features can be assembled from those four with total weight larger than one. (Real data have no “true support”, and the conditions are sufficient, not necessary: OMP did select those four features first. The point is that guarantees of this kind describe nearly orthogonal designs, and real features are correlated.)

10.4.3 An experiment: recovering a known support¶

To test the theory we need a world where the support is known, so the next experiment is constructed: a Gaussian design with p=100p = 100p=100 features, a true support of s=5s = 5s=5 features chosen at random with weights of random sign and magnitude between 1 and 2, and no noise (the setting of Theorem 10.4). For each number of examples nnn and 200 random worlds we ask whether the method finds the exact support. For OMP we run sss steps. For the lasso, which we define in the next section, we follow its whole regularization path (computed exactly by the LARS algorithm, Section 10.5.5) and ask whether some value of the penalty gives exactly the true support: a generous criterion, which gives the lasso the benefit of an oracle for the choice of λ\lambdaλ.

def recovery_experiment(ns, p=100, s=5, reps=200, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = {"OMP": [], "lasso path (best lambda)": []}
    for n in ns:
        ok_omp = ok_las = 0
        for _ in range(reps):
            X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
            X /= np.linalg.norm(X, axis=0)                      # unit-norm columns, as in Theorem 10.4
            S0 = set(rng.choice(p, s, replace=False).tolist())
            w = np.zeros(p)
            w[list(S0)] = rng.choice([-1, 1], s) * (1 + rng.random(s))
            y = X @ w
            ok_omp += set(omp(X, y, s)[0]) == S0
            _, _, coefs = lars_path(X, y, method="lasso")
            ok_las += any(set(np.flatnonzero(np.abs(coefs[:, k]) > 1e-10).tolist()) == S0 for k in range(coefs.shape[1]))
        out["OMP"].append(ok_omp / reps)
        out["lasso path (best lambda)"].append(ok_las / reps)
    return out


ns_rec = [10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60]
t0 = time.time()
rec = recovery_experiment(ns_rec)
print(pd.DataFrame({"n": ns_rec, **rec}).round(2).to_string(index=False))
print(f"({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")

    ax.plot(ns_rec, rec["lasso path (best lambda)"], "s--", color=VERMILION, label=r"lasso path, best $\lambda$ (oracle)")
    ax.axvline(5 * np.log(100), color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
    ax.text(5 * np.log(100) + 0.5, 0.05, r"$s\ln p$", color="gray")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of examples $n$", ylabel="probability of recovering the exact support",

    ax.legend(frameon=False)

figure_10_2()

Figure 10.2 shows a sharp transition from failure to success as nnn grows, for both methods. OMP recovers the support in 58%58\%58% of the worlds at n=25n=25n=25 and in 96%96\%96% at n=40n=40n=40; the lasso path, with the oracle choice of λ\lambdaλ, in 94%94\%94% at n=25n=25n=25 and in all the worlds from n=30n=30n=30. Both transitions happen at a small multiple of sln⁡p=23s\ln p = 23slnp=23, not at s2ln⁡p≈115s^2\ln p\approx 115s2lnp≈115 that the coherence condition of Corollary 10.5 would require: the corollary is a sufficient condition, and a conservative one. In this experiment the convex method needs fewer examples than the greedy one, but we gave it the oracle value of λ\lambdaλ; choosing λ\lambdaλ from the data is a harder problem, which we take up in Section 10.7.

10.5 The lasso¶

10.5.1 From the count to the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm¶

Greedy methods are fast but have no certificate of optimality. A different route is to replace the non-convex count ∥w∥0\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0∥w∥0​ by the closest convex function, the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm ∥w∥1=∑j∣wj∣\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1 = \sum_j\lvert w_j\rvert∥w∥1​=∑j​∣wj​∣ (it is the convex envelope of ∥⋅∥0\lVert\cdot\rVert_0∥⋅∥0​ on the cube [−1,1]p[-1,1]^p[−1,1]p). The resulting estimator was introduced by Tibshirani (1996) with the name lasso (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator), and, in the signal-processing literature, as basis pursuit denoising (Chen, Donoho and Saunders, 1998).

Definition 10.2 (the lasso)

For λ≥0\lambda\ge 0λ≥0 the lasso estimator is

w^λ∈arg⁡min⁡w∈Rp Fλ(w),Fλ(w)=12n∥y−Xw∥2+λ∥w∥1,(10.4)\hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambda\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^p}\ F_\lambda(\mathbf{w}),\qquad F_\lambda(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1, \tag{10.4}w^λ​∈argw∈Rpmin​ Fλ​(w),Fλ​(w)=2n1​∥y−Xw∥2+λ∥w∥1​,(10.4)
(7)

for centered y\mathbf{y}y and standardized columns of X\mathbf{X}X (the intercept is the mean of y\mathbf{y}y and is not penalized, as in Lemma 6.3). This is the parametrization of scikit-learn, where λ\lambdaλ is called alpha. The equivalent constrained form minimizes 12n∥y−Xw∥2\frac{1}{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^22n1​∥y−Xw∥2 subject to ∥w∥1≤t\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1\le t∥w∥1​≤t.

The problem is convex (a convex quadratic plus a norm) but not differentiable at the points where a coordinate is zero, which is exactly where the interesting solutions live. The penalized and the constrained form are equivalent in the usual sense of Lagrangian duality: for each λ\lambdaλ there is a ttt with the same solution (and conversely). The geometry explains why the solution has zeros. In the constrained form, the least-squares solution w^OLS\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathrm{OLS}}w^OLS​ is the center of elliptical contours of the training error, and the solution is the first point of the constraint set that the growing ellipses touch. The ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ ball is round, and the contact point has, in general, all coordinates non-zero; the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ ball has corners on the coordinate axes, which stick out, and the ellipses are likely to touch it at a corner, where some coordinates are exactly zero. We draw it with two real features of the Diabetes data, the body mass index and the age (the contours are those of the actual training error; the size of the ball is 60%60\%60% of the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ or ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ norm of the least-squares solution).

from scipy.optimize import brentq

pair = [feat.index("bmi"), feat.index("age")]
A2 = Zd[:, pair]
w_ols2 = np.linalg.lstsq(A2, yc, rcond=None)[0]


def lasso_at_fraction(fraction):
    """Lasso on the pair with ||w||_1 = fraction * ||w_ols||_1 (bisection on lambda)."""
    target = fraction * np.abs(w_ols2).sum()
    f = lambda lam: np.abs(Lasso(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=100000).fit(A2, yc).coef_).sum() - target
    lam = brentq(f, 1e-6, 100.0)
    return Lasso(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=100000).fit(A2, yc).coef_


def ridge_at_fraction(fraction):
    target = fraction * np.linalg.norm(w_ols2)
    f = lambda lam: np.linalg.norm(Ridge(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False).fit(A2, yc).coef_) - target
    lam = brentq(f, 1e-8, 1e6)
    return Ridge(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False).fit(A2, yc).coef_


w_las2, w_rid2 = lasso_at_fraction(0.6), ridge_at_fraction(0.6)
print("least squares (bmi, age):", np.round(w_ols2, 2))
print("lasso, 60% of the l1 norm:", np.round(w_las2, 2), "(age is exactly zero)" if w_las2[1] == 0 else "")
print("ridge, 60% of the l2 norm:", np.round(w_rid2, 2))

lasso, 60% of the l1 norm: [31.18  0.  ] (age is exactly zero)
ridge, 60% of the l2 norm: [26.42  6.26]

def figure_10_3():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12.5, 4.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.7]})
    ax = axes[0]
    th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
    ax.plot([-1, 1], [0, 0], color=PURPLE, lw=3, label=r"$\ell_0$: $\|w\|_0\leq 1$")
    ax.plot([0, 0], [-1, 1], color=PURPLE, lw=3)
    q = 0.5
    t = np.linspace(-1, 1, 801)
    ax.plot(t, (1 - np.abs(t) ** q) ** (1 / q), color=GREEN, lw=1.6, label=r"$\ell_{1/2}$ (not convex)")
    ax.plot(t, -(1 - np.abs(t) ** q) ** (1 / q), color=GREEN, lw=1.6)

    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=8.5)

    ax.plot(*w_rid2, "s", color=BLUE, ms=8, label="ridge: both non-zero")
    ax.set(xlim=(-5, 62), ylim=(-14, 22), aspect="equal", xlabel=r"weight of bmi", ylabel=r"weight of age", title="(b) real contours: Diabetes, bmi and age")

figure_10_3()

Panel (a) of Figure 10.3 shows the unit balls. The “ℓ0\ell_0ℓ0​ ball” is the cross formed by the two axes; the ℓ1/2\ell_{1/2}ℓ1/2​ ball is a non-convex star that hugs the cross; the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ ball is the diamond with corners on the axes, the smallest convex set that contains the cross; the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ ball is round. Panel (b) uses real contours. The least-squares solution (star) gives 44.7 to the body mass index and 7.3 to the age. With 60%60\%60% of the norm, the lasso solution is (31.2,0)(31.2, 0)(31.2,0), exactly at the corner of the diamond on the axis of the body mass index: the age is eliminated. The ridge solution is (26.4,6.3)(26.4, 6.3)(26.4,6.3), on the circle, with both weights non-zero. The corner is not a certainty (with a different orientation of the ellipses, or a larger budget, the contact would be on an edge, and both weights would be non-zero), but the geometry shows why zeros are typical for the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ ball and impossible in general for the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ ball; in ppp dimensions the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ ball has 2p2p2p corners and many low-dimensional faces, so the ellipses meet it at a point with many zero coordinates with positive probability.

10.5.2 The orthonormal case: soft-thresholding¶

When the columns are orthonormal in the sense 1nX⊤X=I\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}n1​X⊤X=I, the lasso has a closed form, and it shows in one line the difference between the three ways of penalizing. With w^jOLS=1nxj⊤y\hat w^{\mathrm{OLS}}_j = \frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{y}w^jOLS​=n1​xj⊤​y the least-squares coefficients, the objective separates into ppp one-dimensional problems, since 12n∥y−Xw∥2=const+12∑j(wj−w^jOLS)2\frac1{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = \text{const} + \frac12\sum_j(w_j-\hat w_j^{\mathrm{OLS}})^22n1​∥y−Xw∥2=const+21​∑j​(wj​−w^jOLS​)2.

Proposition 10.6 (soft-thresholding). For 1nX⊤X=I\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{I}n1​X⊤X=I the lasso solution is w^j=Sλ(w^jOLS)\hat w_j = S_\lambda(\hat w_j^{\mathrm{OLS}})w^j​=Sλ​(w^jOLS​) with the soft-thresholding operator

Sλ(z)=sign⁡(z) max⁡(∣z∣−λ,0)={z−λz>λ,0∣z∣≤λ,z+λz<−λ.S_\lambda(z) = \operatorname{sign}(z)\,\max(\lvert z\rvert - \lambda, 0) = \begin{cases} z - \lambda & z>\lambda,\\ 0 & \lvert z\rvert\le\lambda,\\ z+\lambda & z<-\lambda.\end{cases}Sλ​(z)=sign(z)max(∣z∣−λ,0)=⎩⎨⎧​z−λ0z+λ​z>λ,∣z∣≤λ,z<−λ.​
(8)

For comparison, ridge gives w^jOLS/(1+λ)\hat w_j^{\mathrm{OLS}}/(1+\lambda)w^jOLS​/(1+λ) (the same shrinkage factor for every coordinate), and best subset with sss non-zeros keeps the sss coordinates of largest ∣w^jOLS∣\lvert\hat w_j^{\mathrm{OLS}}\rvert∣w^jOLS​∣ unchanged and sets the others to zero (hard thresholding).

Proof

We minimize h(w)=12(w−z)2+λ∣w∣h(w) = \frac12(w-z)^2 + \lambda\lvert w\rverth(w)=21​(w−z)2+λ∣w∣ over w∈Rw\in\mathbb{R}w∈R, with z=w^jOLSz = \hat w^{\mathrm{OLS}}_jz=w^jOLS​. The function is strictly convex, so it has a unique minimizer, characterized by 0∈∂h(w)0\in\partial h(w)0∈∂h(w), where ∂∣w∣={sign⁡(w)}\partial\lvert w\rvert = \{\operatorname{sign}(w)\}∂∣w∣={sign(w)} if w≠0w\ne0w=0 and [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] if w=0w=0w=0. If w>0w>0w>0 the condition is w−z+λ=0w - z + \lambda = 0w−z+λ=0, that is, w=z−λw = z-\lambdaw=z−λ, valid when z>λz>\lambdaz>λ. If w<0w<0w<0 it is w=z+λw = z+\lambdaw=z+λ, valid when z<−λz<-\lambdaz<−λ. If w=0w=0w=0 it requires −z+λg=0-z + \lambda g = 0−z+λg=0 for some g∈[−1,1]g\in[-1,1]g∈[−1,1], that is, ∣z∣≤λ\lvert z\rvert\le\lambda∣z∣≤λ. These three cases cover all zzz and give Sλ(z)S_\lambda(z)Sλ​(z). The ridge case is min⁡12(w−z)2+λ2w2\min\frac12(w-z)^2+\frac\lambda2w^2min21​(w−z)2+2λ​w2, with derivative w−z+λw=0w-z+\lambda w=0w−z+λw=0. For the best subset, the reduction of the residual sum of squares from including coordinate jjj is n2(w^jOLS)2\frac n2(\hat w_j^{\mathrm{OLS}})^22n​(w^jOLS​)2, so the best sss coordinates are the largest in absolute value. □\square□

Worked example 10.1 (by hand). Let 1nX⊤X=I\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{I}n1​X⊤X=I with p=4p=4p=4 and least-squares coefficients w^OLS=(3.0, −1.5, 0.4, −0.2)\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathrm{OLS}} = (3.0,\,-1.5,\,0.4,\,-0.2)w^OLS=(3.0,−1.5,0.4,−0.2). With λ=0.5\lambda = 0.5λ=0.5, soft-thresholding gives (2.5, −1.0, 0, 0)(2.5,\,-1.0,\,0,\,0)(2.5,−1.0,0,0): the two large coefficients are shrunk by 0.5 and the two small ones are eliminated. Ridge with the same λ\lambdaλ gives w^OLS/1.5=(2.0, −1.0, 0.27, −0.13)\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathrm{OLS}}/1.5 = (2.0,\,-1.0,\,0.27,\,-0.13)w^OLS/1.5=(2.0,−1.0,0.27,−0.13): all four remain, none exactly zero. Best subset with s=2s=2s=2 gives (3.0, −1.5, 0, 0)(3.0,\,-1.5,\,0,\,0)(3.0,−1.5,0,0): the same support as the lasso, without the shrinkage. Check with the code below.

def soft(z, lam):
    return np.sign(z) * np.maximum(np.abs(z) - lam, 0.0)


z_ex = np.array([3.0, -1.5, 0.4, -0.2])
lam_ex = 0.5
hard_ex = np.where(np.argsort(np.argsort(-np.abs(z_ex))) < 2, z_ex, 0.0)
print("least squares :", z_ex)
print("lasso (soft)  :", soft(z_ex, lam_ex))
print("ridge         :", np.round(z_ex / (1 + lam_ex), 2))
print("best subset s=2 (hard):", hard_ex)

# The same formulas against scikit-learn on an exactly orthonormal design (QR of a random matrix; constructed).
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(200, 6)))
Xo = Q * np.sqrt(200)                                     # X^T X / n = I
yo = Xo @ np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) + rng.normal(size=200)
yo = yo - yo.mean()
w_ols_o = Xo.T @ yo / 200
for lam in [0.1, 0.4]:
    w_sk = Lasso(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12).fit(Xo, yo).coef_
    print(f"lambda = {lam}: max |scikit-learn - soft-thresholding| = {np.abs(w_sk - soft(w_ols_o, lam)).max():.1e}")

lasso (soft)  : [ 2.5 -1.   0.  -0. ]
ridge         : [ 2.   -1.    0.27 -0.13]

def figure_10_4():
    z = np.linspace(-3, 3, 601)
    lam = 1.0
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.2))
    ax.plot(z, z, color="gray", lw=1, ls=":", label="least squares")
    ax.plot(z, soft(z, lam), color=VERMILION, lw=2.2, label=r"lasso: soft-thresholding, $\lambda=1$")
    ax.plot(z, z / (1 + lam), color=BLUE, lw=2.2, ls="--", label=r"ridge: $z/(1+\lambda)$")
    ax.plot(z, np.where(np.abs(z) > 1.5, z, 0.0), color=GREEN, lw=2.2, ls="-.", label="best subset: hard threshold (at 1.5)")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"least-squares coefficient $\hat w^{\rm OLS}_j$", ylabel="estimate", title="Three ways to treat a coefficient (orthonormal design)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_10_4()

Figure 10.4 contrasts the three treatments of a coefficient. The lasso is zero on [−λ,λ][-\lambda,\lambda][−λ,λ] and shifted towards zero by λ\lambdaλ outside: it is continuous and sparse, and its bias for large coefficients is the constant λ\lambdaλ. Ridge shrinks proportionally and never gives zero. The hard threshold of best-subset selection has no bias for the coefficients that it keeps, but it is discontinuous: a small change in the data can move a coefficient from 0 to 1.5, which makes the selected model unstable. The lasso is the only one of the three that is both sparse and continuous in the data, and it is the one that is a convex problem in the general case. The code checks that scikit-learn’s solver agrees with soft-thresholding on an orthonormal design to machine precision (5×10−165\times10^{-16}5×10−16).

10.5.3 Optimality conditions¶

For a general design there is no closed form, but the same subgradient argument gives a complete characterization of the solutions. Write r=y−Xw\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}r=y−Xw for the residual.

Theorem 10.7 (optimality conditions of the lasso). A vector w\mathbf{w}w minimizes FλF_\lambdaFλ​ if and only if, for every coordinate jjj,

1nxj⊤r=λsign⁡(wj)  if wj≠0,∣1nxj⊤r∣≤λ  if wj=0.(10.5)\frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r} = \lambda\operatorname{sign}(w_j)\ \text{ if } w_j\neq 0,\qquad\Big\lvert\frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}\Big\rvert\le\lambda\ \text{ if } w_j = 0. \tag{10.5}n1​xj⊤​r=λsign(wj​)  if wj​=0,∣∣​n1​xj⊤​r∣∣​≤λ  if wj​=0.(10.5)
(9)

In words: every feature that is in the model has the same absolute correlation λ\lambdaλ with the residual, and every feature that is out has a correlation at most λ\lambdaλ. In particular w^λ=0\hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambda = \mathbf{0}w^λ​=0 if and only if λ≥λmax⁡=1n∥X⊤y∥∞\lambda\ge\lambda_{\max} = \frac1n\lVert\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\rVert_\inftyλ≥λmax​=n1​∥X⊤y∥∞​.

Proof

The function FλF_\lambdaFλ​ is convex, so w\mathbf{w}w is a minimizer if and only if 0∈∂Fλ(w)\mathbf{0}\in\partial F_\lambda(\mathbf{w})0∈∂Fλ​(w). The first term is differentiable with gradient −1nX⊤r-\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{r}−n1​X⊤r, and the subdifferential of a sum of a differentiable convex function and a convex function is the sum of the gradient and the subdifferential, so ∂Fλ(w)=−1nX⊤r+λ ∂∥w∥1\partial F_\lambda(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{r} + \lambda\,\partial\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1∂Fλ​(w)=−n1​X⊤r+λ∂∥w∥1​. The subdifferential of the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm is the product of the sets {sign⁡(wj)}\{\operatorname{sign}(w_j)\}{sign(wj​)} (if wj≠0w_j\ne0wj​=0) and [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] (if wj=0w_j=0wj​=0); the condition 0∈∂Fλ(w)\mathbf{0}\in\partial F_\lambda(\mathbf{w})0∈∂Fλ​(w) coordinate by coordinate is (10.5). For w=0\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}w=0 the residual is y\mathbf{y}y and (10.5) reads ∣1nxj⊤y∣≤λ\lvert\frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{y}\rvert\le\lambda∣n1​xj⊤​y∣≤λ for all jjj. □\square□

The value λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​ is the natural starting point of the regularization path: for larger values the model is empty, and as λ\lambdaλ decreases the feature that is the most correlated with y\mathbf{y}y enters first (it is the first to reach the correlation λ\lambdaλ). Two properties of the solution are worth knowing and are left to the exercises. The fitted values Xw^λ\mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambdaXw^λ​ are always unique (Exercise 10.5), even if the weights are not: with two identical columns, any split of the weight between them has the same fit and the same penalty (Exercise 10.3). The weights are unique when the columns are in “general position” (no n+1n+1n+1 columns on a common affine subspace, Tibshirani, 2013), which holds with probability one for continuous data, and then the solution has at most min⁡(n,p)\min(n,p)min(n,p) non-zero entries. We check (10.5) on the Diabetes data with the solution of scikit-learn.

lam_ex2 = 1.0
w_las = Lasso(alpha=lam_ex2, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-14, max_iter=200000).fit(Zd, yc).coef_
corr_res = Zd.T @ (yc - Zd @ w_las) / n_d
lam_max_d = np.abs(Zd.T @ yc).max() / n_d
print(f"lambda_max = {lam_max_d:.3f} (first feature to enter: {feat[int(np.abs(Zd.T @ yc).argmax())]})")
print(pd.DataFrame({"feature": feat, "weight": w_las, "x_j' r / n": corr_res,
                    "|x_j' r / n| - lambda": np.abs(corr_res) - lam_ex2}).round(4).to_string(index=False))
inside = w_las != 0
print("max |x_j' r / n - lambda sign(w_j)| over the active features:", f"{np.abs(corr_res[inside] - lam_ex2 * np.sign(w_las[inside])).max():.1e}")
print("max |x_j' r / n| over the inactive features, against lambda:", f"{np.abs(corr_res[~inside]).max():.4f} <= {lam_ex2}")

At λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 the solution has nine non-zero weights (s2\texttt{s2}s2 is the only feature out of the model), and the conditions (10.5) hold to 2×10−132\times10^{-13}2×10−13: the nine active features have a correlation with the residual of exactly ±1.0000=λsign⁡(wj)\pm1.0000 = \lambda\operatorname{sign}(w_j)±1.0000=λsign(wj​), and the correlation of s2 is 0.53<λ0.53<\lambda0.53<λ. The value λmax⁡=45.97\lambda_{\max}=45.97λmax​=45.97 is the correlation of bmi with the response, the largest one, so bmi is the first feature to enter. The condition that all the active features have the same correlation with the residual is also the idea of the LARS algorithm (“least angle regression”): it moves the weights so as to keep the active features equally correlated with the residual.

10.5.4 The Bayesian reading: a Laplace prior¶

Section 6.3.5 gave three readings of ridge regression: a penalty, a constraint on the norm, and a Gaussian prior on the weights. The lasso has the same three, with the Laplace (double-exponential) distribution in place of the Gaussian. Suppose y=Xw+ε\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}+\boldsymbol\varepsilony=Xw+ε with εi∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)εi​∼N(0,σ2) and independent prior densities p(wj)=12be−∣wj∣/bp(w_j) = \frac{1}{2b}e^{-\lvert w_j\rvert/b}p(wj​)=2b1​e−∣wj​∣/b. The negative log of the posterior density is, up to a constant, 12σ2∥y−Xw∥2+1b∥w∥1\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + \frac1b\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_12σ21​∥y−Xw∥2+b1​∥w∥1​; multiplying by σ2/n\sigma^2/nσ2/n gives (10.4) with λ=σ2/(nb)\lambda = \sigma^2/(nb)λ=σ2/(nb). The lasso is the maximum a posteriori estimate under the Laplace prior, just as ridge is the MAP estimate under the Gaussian one. The Laplace density has a sharp peak at zero and heavier tails than the Gaussian: it says that most weights are very small and a few are large, which is the prior belief of a sparse model. One caution: it is the MAP, the mode of the posterior, that is sparse; the posterior mean under the Laplace prior (the “Bayesian lasso” of Park and Casella, 2008) is not, since a mean of a continuous distribution is zero with probability zero. The zeros of the lasso come from the mode.

10.5.5 The regularization path¶

As λ\lambdaλ decreases from λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​ to 0 the solution w^λ\hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambdaw^λ​ moves from 0\mathbf{0}0 to the least-squares solution. For the lasso this path is piecewise linear in λ\lambdaλ (Efron, Hastie, Johnstone and Tibshirani, 2004; Osborne, Presnell and Turlach, 2000): between two “knots”, at which a feature enters or leaves the model, the active coefficients change linearly with λ\lambdaλ. The reason is (10.5): on the active set AAA the equation 1nXA⊤(y−XAwA)=λsign⁡(wA)\frac1n\mathbf{X}_A^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}_A\mathbf{w}_A) = \lambda\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}_A)n1​XA⊤​(y−XA​wA​)=λsign(wA​) is linear in (wA,λ)(\mathbf{w}_A, \lambda)(wA​,λ), so wA=(XA⊤XA)−1(XA⊤y−nλsign⁡(wA))\mathbf{w}_A = (\mathbf{X}_A^\top\mathbf{X}_A)^{-1}(\mathbf{X}_A^\top\mathbf{y} - n\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}_A))wA​=(XA⊤​XA​)−1(XA⊤​y−nλsign(wA​)) as long as the active set and the signs do not change. The LARS algorithm computes the knots exactly. We compare the lasso path with the ridge path on the Diabetes data; both are plotted against the fraction of the least-squares norm that they keep, so that the horizontal axes are comparable (1 is least squares, 0 the empty model).

alphas_path, coefs_path, _ = lasso_path(Zd, yc, alphas=np.logspace(np.log10(lam_max_d), np.log10(lam_max_d * 1e-4), 300))
w_ols_d = np.linalg.lstsq(Zd, yc, rcond=None)[0]
frac_lasso = np.abs(coefs_path).sum(axis=0) / np.abs(w_ols_d).sum()
ridge_lams = np.logspace(-3, 5, 300)
coefs_ridge = np.array([Ridge(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False).fit(Zd, yc).coef_ for lam in ridge_lams]).T
frac_ridge = np.linalg.norm(coefs_ridge, axis=0) / np.linalg.norm(w_ols_d)

# order of entry along the lasso path
entry = []
for k in range(coefs_path.shape[1]):
    for j in np.flatnonzero(coefs_path[:, k]):
        if feat[j] not in entry:
            entry.append(feat[j])
print("order of entry along the lasso path:", entry)
print("order of entry in OMP              :", [feat[j] for j in order_omp])
print("order of entry in forward selection:", [feat[j] for j in order_fwd])
print("correlation of each feature with the response:", ", ".join(f"{f} {np.corrcoef(Zd[:, j], yc)[0, 1]:+.2f}" for j, f in enumerate(feat)))

# Exact knots (LARS) and a check of piecewise linearity: the solution halfway between two knots is the average of the knots.
lars_alphas, lars_active, lars_coefs = lars_path(Zd, yc, method="lasso")
print(f"the exact path has {lars_coefs.shape[1]} knots; lambda at the knots: {np.round(lars_alphas[:6], 2)} ...")
k0 = 3
lam_mid = (lars_alphas[k0] + lars_alphas[k0 + 1]) / 2
w_mid_direct = Lasso(alpha=lam_mid, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-14, max_iter=200000).fit(Zd, yc).coef_
w_mid_interp = (lars_coefs[:, k0] + lars_coefs[:, k0 + 1]) / 2
print(f"max |solution at the midpoint - average of the two knots| = {np.abs(w_mid_direct - w_mid_interp).max():.1e}")

# What happens at each knot: which feature enters (+) or leaves (-) the model as lambda falls below the knot.
# (The column k of lars_coefs is the solution AT lambda_k: an entering feature is still zero there.)
nonzero = np.abs(lars_coefs) > 1e-12
events = []
for k in range(lars_coefs.shape[1] - 1):
    enters = [f"+{feat[j]}" for j in range(p_d) if not nonzero[j, k] and nonzero[j, k + 1]]
    leaves = [f"-{feat[j]}" for j in range(p_d) if k > 0 and nonzero[j, k - 1] and not nonzero[j, k]]
    events.append({"knot": k, "lambda": lars_alphas[k], "enters (+) / leaves (-)": " ".join(enters + leaves),
                   "features in the model just below the knot": int((nonzero[:, k] | nonzero[:, k + 1]).sum())})
print(pd.DataFrame(events).round(2).to_string(index=False))

The exact path has 15 knots (the last one is least squares), and the table of events tells the story of the Diabetes features. bmi enters at λmax⁡=45.97\lambda_{\max}=45.97λmax​=45.97, then s5, bp, s3 and sex one after the other, as in forward selection and OMP. The sixth entry is instructive: s2 enters at λ=4.12\lambda=4.12λ=4.12, is joined by s1 at 3.73 and leaves at 3.64: the two features have a correlation of 0.89, so they are interchangeable for the fit, and the lasso hands the weight from one to the other. s2 returns at λ=0.31\lambda=0.31λ=0.31, and s3 leaves the model at 0.13 to come back at 0.08 with the opposite sign. So the path is not monotone: a feature can leave the model as λ\lambdaλ decreases, and the coefficient of s3, negative for most of the path (-12 at its lowest), is positive at the end (its least-squares weight is +5.5). Panel (b) of Figure 10.5 shows the contrast with ridge: all the coefficients are non-zero from the first value of λ\lambdaλ and move smoothly. Two features are noteworthy in both panels. s1 has a positive correlation with the response (+0.18) and a negative least-squares weight (-44.1); the same collinearity of Section 6.2.4 acts here, and s1 and s2 are the features that take the extreme values at the end of both paths. And the check of piecewise linearity is exact: the lasso solution halfway between two knots is the average of the solutions at the knots, to 3×10−143\times10^{-14}3×10−14.

10.5.6 The price of shrinkage, and how to remove it¶

Soft-thresholding shrinks every surviving coefficient by λ\lambdaλ, including the large ones, which are certainly in the model. The lasso estimates of the large coefficients are therefore biased towards zero by an amount that does not decrease as the coefficient grows (Proposition 10.6; compare the hard threshold, which leaves large coefficients intact). A simple remedy is refitting: use the lasso to select the support and then fit ordinary least squares on the selected features (a version of the “relaxed lasso” of Meinshausen, 2007). The coefficients lose their shrinkage, and gain variance; whether the exchange is favorable depends on the problem. Other remedies (the adaptive lasso, SCAD, MCP) are in the further reading. We compare the coefficients at the value of λ\lambdaλ chosen by cross-validation in Section 10.7.1; the code is there.

10.6 Algorithms for the lasso¶

The lasso objective (10.4) is a sum F=g+hF = g + hF=g+h of a smooth convex function, g(w)=12n∥y−Xw∥2g(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2g(w)=2n1​∥y−Xw∥2, whose gradient ∇g(w)=−1nX⊤(y−Xw)\nabla g(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w})∇g(w)=−n1​X⊤(y−Xw) is LLL-Lipschitz with L=λmax⁡(1nX⊤X)L = \lambda_{\max}(\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})L=λmax​(n1​X⊤X) (Section 7.2), and a convex function that is not differentiable, h(w)=λ∥w∥1h(\mathbf{w}) = \lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1h(w)=λ∥w∥1​. The methods of Chapter 7 handle the first part and the non-smooth part needs something new. We look at three methods, in the order of how closely they use the structure of hhh.

10.6.1 The subgradient method does not give zeros¶

The simplest idea is to apply the subgradient method of Section 8.5.1: wk+1=wk−ηk(∇g(wk)+λsign⁡(wk))\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta_k\big(\nabla g(\mathbf{w}_k) + \lambda\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}_k)\big)wk+1​=wk​−ηk​(∇g(wk​)+λsign(wk​)), with sign⁡(0)=0\operatorname{sign}(0) = 0sign(0)=0 and a decreasing step ηk∝1/k\eta_k\propto1/\sqrt{k}ηk​∝1/k​. It converges, slowly (the guarantee for a general non-smooth convex function is O(1/k)O(1/\sqrt{k})O(1/k​) for the best iterate, and Theorem 8.6 gives O(ln⁡k/k)O(\ln k/k)O(lnk/k) in the strongly convex case with the right step), but its main defect is different. A coordinate that has to be exactly zero at the solution is, at each iteration, moved by the step ηkλ\eta_k\lambdaηk​λ away from zero and then back: the iterates oscillate around the kink and are almost never exactly zero. A method designed to find sparse solutions that returns dense iterates is not useful. We shall measure this below.

10.6.2 Coordinate descent¶

Coordinate descent minimizes FFF over one coordinate at a time, keeping the others fixed. Let cj=1n∥xj∥2c_j = \frac1n\lVert\mathbf{x}_j\rVert^2cj​=n1​∥xj​∥2 (=1=1=1 for standardized columns) and let r−j=y−∑k≠jxkwk\mathbf{r}_{-j} = \mathbf{y}-\sum_{k\ne j}\mathbf{x}_kw_kr−j​=y−∑k=j​xk​wk​ be the partial residual, the residual that we would have without the contribution of feature jjj.

Proposition 10.8 (coordinate update). The minimizer of FλF_\lambdaFλ​ over wjw_jwj​, the other coordinates being fixed, is

wj ← Sλ(ρj)cj,ρj=1nxj⊤r−j.w_j\ \leftarrow\ \frac{S_\lambda(\rho_j)}{c_j},\qquad\rho_j = \frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}_{-j}.wj​ ← cj​Sλ​(ρj​)​,ρj​=n1​xj⊤​r−j​.
(10)
Proof

As a function of wjw_jwj​ alone, Fλ=12n∥r−j−xjwj∥2+λ∣wj∣+const=12cjwj2−ρjwj+λ∣wj∣+const′=cj2(wj−ρj/cj)2+λ∣wj∣+const′′F_\lambda = \frac{1}{2n}\lVert\mathbf{r}_{-j} - \mathbf{x}_jw_j\rVert^2 + \lambda\lvert w_j\rvert + \text{const} = \frac12c_jw_j^2 - \rho_jw_j + \lambda\lvert w_j\rvert + \text{const}' = \frac{c_j}2\big(w_j - \rho_j/c_j\big)^2 + \lambda\lvert w_j\rvert + \text{const}''Fλ​=2n1​∥r−j​−xj​wj​∥2+λ∣wj​∣+const=21​cj​wj2​−ρj​wj​+λ∣wj​∣+const′=2cj​​(wj​−ρj​/cj​)2+λ∣wj​∣+const′′. This is the one-dimensional problem of Proposition 10.6 with z=ρj/cjz = \rho_j/c_jz=ρj​/cj​ and threshold λ/cj\lambda/c_jλ/cj​, whose solution is Sλ/cj(ρj/cj)=Sλ(ρj)/cjS_{\lambda/c_j}(\rho_j/c_j) = S_\lambda(\rho_j)/c_jSλ/cj​​(ρj​/cj​)=Sλ​(ρj​)/cj​. □\square□

An update costs O(n)O(n)O(n) if the residual r\mathbf{r}r is maintained: ρj=1nxj⊤r+cjwj\rho_j = \frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r} + c_jw_jρj​=n1​xj⊤​r+cj​wj​ (add back the contribution of the feature) and, after the update, r←r−xj(wjnew−wjold)\mathbf{r}\leftarrow\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{x}_j(w_j^{\mathrm{new}} - w_j^{\mathrm{old}})r←r−xj​(wjnew​−wjold​). A sweep over all the coordinates costs O(np)O(np)O(np), the cost of one gradient. A coordinate that is zero and stays zero costs only its inner product. Since the non-smooth part hhh is a sum of functions of single coordinates, the algorithm converges to a minimizer (Tseng, 2001; for a non-separable non-smooth part, coordinate descent can get stuck). With a warm start (use the solution for λk\lambda_kλk​ as the starting point for λk+1<λk\lambda_{k+1}<\lambda_kλk+1​<λk​) the whole path is computed in not much more time than a single fit; this is the algorithm of the glmnet package (Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani, 2010), and the one behind scikit-learn’s Lasso and lasso_path. It is the same idea as the dual coordinate descent of Section 8.5.2, applied to the primal problem.

10.6.3 Proximal gradient (ISTA, FISTA)¶

The second method uses hhh through its proximal operator, prox⁡ηh(v)=arg⁡min⁡u { h(u)+12η∥u−v∥2 }\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(\mathbf{v}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}}\ \{\,h(\mathbf{u}) + \frac1{2\eta}\lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\rVert^2\,\}proxηh​(v)=argminu​ {h(u)+2η1​∥u−v∥2}.

Proposition 10.9 (the proximal operator of the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm). For h=λ∥⋅∥1h = \lambda\lVert\cdot\rVert_1h=λ∥⋅∥1​, prox⁡ηh(v)=Sηλ(v)\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(\mathbf{v}) = S_{\eta\lambda}(\mathbf{v})proxηh​(v)=Sηλ​(v), soft-thresholding applied to each coordinate with threshold ηλ\eta\lambdaηλ.

Proof. The objective λ∥u∥1+12η∥u−v∥2\lambda\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert_1 + \frac1{2\eta}\lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\rVert^2λ∥u∥1​+2η1​∥u−v∥2 is a sum over coordinates of λ∣uj∣+12η(uj−vj)2\lambda\lvert u_j\rvert + \frac1{2\eta}(u_j-v_j)^2λ∣uj​∣+2η1​(uj​−vj​)2, and each term is 1η\frac1\etaη1​ times the problem of Proposition 10.6 with threshold ηλ\eta\lambdaηλ. □\square□

The proximal gradient method takes a gradient step on the smooth part and then applies the proximal operator of the non-smooth part:

wk+1=Sηλ(wk−η∇g(wk)).(10.6)\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = S_{\eta\lambda}\big(\mathbf{w}_k - \eta\nabla g(\mathbf{w}_k)\big). \tag{10.6}wk+1​=Sηλ​(wk​−η∇g(wk​)).(10.6)
(11)

With soft-thresholding this is called ISTA (iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm). Its meaning is the one of gradient descent in Section 7.3: by the descent lemma (Proposition 7.2), g(u)≤g(wk)+∇g(wk)⊤(u−wk)+L2∥u−wk∥2g(\mathbf{u})\le g(\mathbf{w}_k) + \nabla g(\mathbf{w}_k)^\top(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{w}_k) + \frac L2\lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{w}_k\rVert^2g(u)≤g(wk​)+∇g(wk​)⊤(u−wk​)+2L​∥u−wk​∥2, and (10.6) with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L minimizes this quadratic upper bound plus the exact hhh. The step is a gradient step with a soft-threshold, and so, unlike the subgradient method, it produces exact zeros.

Theorem 10.10 (proximal gradient). Let ggg be convex and LLL-smooth, hhh convex, and 0<η≤1/L0<\eta\le1/L0<η≤1/L. Then the iterates of (10.6) satisfy F(wk+1)≤F(wk)−12η∥wk+1−wk∥2F(\mathbf{w}_{k+1})\le F(\mathbf{w}_k) - \frac1{2\eta}\lVert\mathbf{w}_{k+1}-\mathbf{w}_k\rVert^2F(wk+1​)≤F(wk​)−2η1​∥wk+1​−wk​∥2, and for every minimizer w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗,

F(wk)−F(w∗)≤∥w0−w∗∥22ηk.F(\mathbf{w}_k) - F(\mathbf{w}^\ast)\le\frac{\lVert\mathbf{w}_0-\mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2}{2\eta k}.F(wk​)−F(w∗)≤2ηk∥w0​−w∗∥2​.
(12)
Proof

Write w+=wk+1\mathbf{w}^+ = \mathbf{w}_{k+1}w+=wk+1​, w=wk\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}_kw=wk​. Step 1: an upper bound for ggg. By the descent lemma and η≤1/L\eta\le1/Lη≤1/L, g(w+)≤g(w)+∇g(w)⊤(w+−w)+12η∥w+−w∥2g(\mathbf{w}^+)\le g(\mathbf{w}) + \nabla g(\mathbf{w})^\top(\mathbf{w}^+-\mathbf{w}) + \frac1{2\eta}\lVert\mathbf{w}^+-\mathbf{w}\rVert^2g(w+)≤g(w)+∇g(w)⊤(w+−w)+2η1​∥w+−w∥2. By convexity, g(w)≤g(z)+∇g(w)⊤(w−z)g(\mathbf{w})\le g(\mathbf{z}) + \nabla g(\mathbf{w})^\top(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{z})g(w)≤g(z)+∇g(w)⊤(w−z) for any z\mathbf{z}z. Adding the two, g(w+)≤g(z)+∇g(w)⊤(w+−z)+12η∥w+−w∥2g(\mathbf{w}^+)\le g(\mathbf{z}) + \nabla g(\mathbf{w})^\top(\mathbf{w}^+-\mathbf{z}) + \frac1{2\eta}\lVert\mathbf{w}^+-\mathbf{w}\rVert^2g(w+)≤g(z)+∇g(w)⊤(w+−z)+2η1​∥w+−w∥2. The point w+\mathbf{w}^+w+ minimizes h(u)+12η∥u−(w−η∇g(w))∥2h(\mathbf{u}) + \frac1{2\eta}\lVert\mathbf{u}-(\mathbf{w}-\eta\nabla g(\mathbf{w}))\rVert^2h(u)+2η1​∥u−(w−η∇g(w))∥2, so 1η(w−w+)−∇g(w)∈∂h(w+)\frac1\eta(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^+) - \nabla g(\mathbf{w})\in\partial h(\mathbf{w}^+)η1​(w−w+)−∇g(w)∈∂h(w+), and the subgradient inequality gives h(z)≥h(w+)+(1η(w−w+)−∇g(w))⊤(z−w+)h(\mathbf{z})\ge h(\mathbf{w}^+) + \big(\frac1\eta(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^+) - \nabla g(\mathbf{w})\big)^\top(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{w}^+)h(z)≥h(w+)+(η1​(w−w+)−∇g(w))⊤(z−w+). F(w+)≤F(z)+12η(∥w+−w∥2−2(w−w+)⊤(z−w+))=F(z)+12η(∥w−z∥2−∥w+−z∥2),F(\mathbf{w}^+)\le F(\mathbf{z}) + \frac1{2\eta}\Big(\lVert\mathbf{w}^+-\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 - 2(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^+)^\top(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{w}^+)\Big) = F(\mathbf{z}) + \frac1{2\eta}\Big(\lVert\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{z}\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf{w}^+-\mathbf{z}\rVert^2\Big),F(w+)≤F(z)+2η1​(∥w+−w∥2−2(w−w+)⊤(z−w+))=F(z)+2η1​(∥w−z∥2−∥w+−z∥2),

where the last equality expands ∥w−z∥2=∥(w−w+)+(w+−z)∥2\lVert\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{z}\rVert^2 = \lVert(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^+) + (\mathbf{w}^+-\mathbf{z})\rVert^2∥w−z∥2=∥(w−w+)+(w+−z)∥2. Taking z=w\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{w}z=w gives the decrease of FFF; taking z=w∗\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{w}^\astz=w∗ and summing over k=0,…,K−1k = 0,\dots,K-1k=0,…,K−1, the right-hand sides telescope: ∑k<K(F(wk+1)−F∗)≤12η∥w0−w∗∥2\sum_{k<K}\big(F(\mathbf{w}_{k+1}) - F^\ast\big)\le\frac1{2\eta}\lVert\mathbf{w}_0-\mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2∑k<K​(F(wk+1​)−F∗)≤2η1​∥w0​−w∗∥2. Since F(wk)F(\mathbf{w}_k)F(wk​) is non-increasing, K(F(wK)−F∗)≤∑k<K(F(wk+1)−F∗)K\big(F(\mathbf{w}_K)-F^\ast\big)\le\sum_{k<K}\big(F(\mathbf{w}_{k+1})-F^\ast\big)K(F(wK​)−F∗)≤∑k<K​(F(wk+1​)−F∗), which is the claim. □\square□

The rate is that of gradient descent on a smooth convex function (Theorem 7.4): the non-smooth part costs nothing in the rate, provided its proximal operator is cheap. As in Chapter 7, momentum accelerates it: FISTA (Beck and Teboulle, 2009) applies (10.6) at the extrapolated point vk=wk+tk−1−1tk(wk−wk−1)\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{w}_k + \frac{t_{k-1}-1}{t_k}(\mathbf{w}_k-\mathbf{w}_{k-1})vk​=wk​+tk​tk−1​−1​(wk​−wk−1​) with tk+1=(1+1+4tk2)/2t_{k+1} = \big(1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}\big)/2tk+1​=(1+1+4tk2​​)/2, and achieves O(1/k2)O(1/k^2)O(1/k2), the rate of Nesterov’s method (Theorem 7.9). When ggg is strongly convex, as it is for the Diabetes data (μ=0.0094\mu = 0.0094μ=0.0094 for the standardized features, with L=3.92L = 3.92L=3.92, so κ=418\kappa = 418κ=418, the number of Section 7.2), both converge linearly, with the factor of Theorem 7.5 for ISTA.

10.6.4 A comparison on the Diabetes data¶

We solve the lasso with λ=5\lambda = 5λ=5 on the standardized Diabetes training set with the four methods: the subgradient method with step c/kc/\sqrt{k}c/k​ for four values of ccc, ISTA and FISTA with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L, and coordinate descent. The reference solution F∗F^\astF∗ comes from 2,000 sweeps of coordinate descent (checked below against scikit-learn). One iteration of ISTA, FISTA or the subgradient method and one sweep of coordinate descent cost the same, O(np)O(np)O(np), so the comparison is per unit of work.

def lasso_obj(Z, y, w, lam):
    r = y - Z @ w
    return float(r @ r) / (2 * len(y)) + lam * np.abs(w).sum()


def lasso_cd(Z, y, lam, w0=None, n_sweeps=200):
    """Cyclic coordinate descent (Proposition 10.8). Returns w and, per sweep, the objective and the support."""
    n, p = Z.shape
    w = np.zeros(p) if w0 is None else w0.copy()
    r = y - Z @ w
    c = (Z ** 2).sum(axis=0) / n
    objs, supports = [], []
    for _ in range(n_sweeps):
        for j in range(p):
            rho = Z[:, j] @ r / n + c[j] * w[j]
            w_new = soft(rho, lam) / c[j]
            if w_new != w[j]:
                r += Z[:, j] * (w[j] - w_new)
                w[j] = w_new
        objs.append(lasso_obj(Z, y, w, lam))
        supports.append(w != 0)
    return w, np.array(objs), np.array(supports)


def lasso_prox_grad(Z, y, lam, eta, n_iter=2000, accelerated=False):
    """ISTA (10.6), or FISTA when accelerated=True."""
    n, p = Z.shape
    w = np.zeros(p)
    v, t = w.copy(), 1.0
    objs, supports = [], []
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        grad = -Z.T @ (y - Z @ v) / n
        w_new = soft(v - eta * grad, eta * lam)
        if accelerated:
            t_new = (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 4 * t * t)) / 2
            v = w_new + (t - 1) / t_new * (w_new - w)
            t = t_new
        else:
            v = w_new
        w = w_new
        objs.append(lasso_obj(Z, y, w, lam))
        supports.append(w != 0)
    return w, np.array(objs), np.array(supports)


def lasso_subgradient(Z, y, lam, c, n_iter=2000):
    n, p = Z.shape
    w = np.zeros(p)
    objs, supports = [], []
    for k in range(n_iter):
        g = -Z.T @ (y - Z @ w) / n + lam * np.sign(w)
        w = w - c / np.sqrt(k + 1) * g
        objs.append(lasso_obj(Z, y, w, lam))
        supports.append(w != 0)
    return w, np.array(objs), np.array(supports)


lam_s = 5.0
L_d = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Zd.T @ Zd / n_d).max()
mu_d = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Zd.T @ Zd / n_d).min()
w_star, objs_cd_long, _ = lasso_cd(Zd, yc, lam_s, n_sweeps=2000)
F_star = lasso_obj(Zd, yc, w_star, lam_s)
w_sk1 = Lasso(alpha=lam_s, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-14, max_iter=200000).fit(Zd, yc).coef_
print(f"L = {L_d:.3f}, mu = {mu_d:.4f}, kappa = {L_d / mu_d:.0f}; F* = {F_star:.6f}; non-zeros at the solution: {int((w_star != 0).sum())}")
print(f"our coordinate descent vs scikit-learn: max |difference of the weights| = {np.abs(w_star - w_sk1).max():.1e}")
S_star = np.flatnonzero(w_star)
ev_S = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Zd[:, S_star].T @ Zd[:, S_star] / n_d)
print(f"support of the solution: {', '.join(feat[j] for j in S_star)}; restricted to it, L_S = {ev_S.max():.2f}, mu_S = {ev_S.min():.3f}, kappa_S = {ev_S.max() / ev_S.min():.1f}")

runs = {}
runs["coordinate descent"] = lasso_cd(Zd, yc, lam_s, n_sweeps=200)[1:]
runs["ISTA"] = lasso_prox_grad(Zd, yc, lam_s, 1 / L_d)[1:]
runs["FISTA"] = lasso_prox_grad(Zd, yc, lam_s, 1 / L_d, accelerated=True)[1:]
for c_ in [0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0]:
    runs[f"subgradient, c={c_}"] = lasso_subgradient(Zd, yc, lam_s, c_)[1:]

supp_star = w_star != 0
rows = []
for name, (objs, supports) in runs.items():
    gap = objs - F_star
    row = {"method": name, "gap after 200 iterations": gap[199]}
    for tol in [1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9]:
        hit = np.flatnonzero(gap <= tol)
        row[f"iterations to {tol:.0e}"] = int(hit[0]) + 1 if len(hit) else "not reached"
    mism = (supports != supp_star).any(axis=1)
    row["iteration after which the support is exact"] = "never" if mism[-1] else (int(np.flatnonzero(mism).max()) + 2 if mism.any() else 1)
    row["non-zeros at the end"] = int(supports[-1].sum())
    rows.append(row)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2e}"))
