figure_10_6()

Figure 10.6 and the table tell the same story. Coordinate descent is the fastest: after 8 sweeps the gap is below 10-3, after 10 below 10-6 and after 15 below 10-9, and the support is exact from the second sweep on, because a coordinate that the soft-threshold sets to zero stays at zero. ISTA needs 31, 61 and 92 iterations for the same three accuracies and identifies the support after 15; FISTA is faster at the beginning (22 iterations to 10-3, against 31) but its gap is not monotone (the ripples in panel (a) are the momentum, as in Section 7.5) and for high accuracy it is no better than ISTA (93 against 92 iterations to 10-9). The reason is visible in the printed conditioning: once the support is identified, both methods are minimizing a function of the five active coordinates only, whose condition number is κS≈5\kappa_S\approx 5κS​≈5 and not the κ=418\kappa = 418κ=418 of the whole problem, so plain gradient steps already converge linearly and fast; the acceleration of Theorem 7.9 pays when the problem is badly conditioned, and here it is not. The subgradient method is in a different league: after 2,000 iterations none of the four step constants has reached a gap of 10-3 (after 200 iterations the best of them, c=0.3c=0.3c=0.3, is at 0.58, and the largest step oscillates at a gap of order one), and, as panel (b) shows, it never produces a zero: it keeps all ten coordinates non-zero while the solution has five. For the lasso the correct choice is a method that uses the soft-threshold, which is what the proximal and coordinate methods do. (The 10 columns of Diabetes make every method fast; with ppp in the thousands the cost per sweep, O(np)O(np)O(np), and the identification of the active set are what matter, and coordinate descent with warm starts along the path is the standard solver.)

10.7 Choosing λ\lambdaλ, and what sparsity buys¶

10.7.1 Cross-validation and the one-standard-error rule¶

The penalty λ\lambdaλ plays for the lasso the role of the size kkk for subset selection: too large gives a model that is too small and biased, too small a model that overfits. We choose it as in Chapter 5, with 10-fold cross-validation, repeating the standardization in each fold (the lasso is also computed on the whole path in each fold, from the same grid of 60 values of λ\lambdaλ, which makes the folds comparable). The one-standard-error rule of Section 5.4.1 chooses the largest λ\lambdaλ (the sparsest model) whose error is within one standard error of the minimum.

def cv_lasso_path(X, y, alphas, n_folds=10, seed=SEED):
    """10-fold CV error of the lasso along a grid of penalties; standardization repeated inside each fold."""
    kf = KFold(n_folds, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    errs = np.zeros((n_folds, len(alphas)))
    for f, (tr, va) in enumerate(kf.split(X)):
        sc = StandardScaler().fit(X[tr])
        A, B = sc.transform(X[tr]), sc.transform(X[va])
        ym = y[tr].mean()
        _, coefs, _ = lasso_path(A, y[tr] - ym, alphas=alphas, tol=1e-9, max_iter=20000)
        pred = B @ coefs + ym
        errs[f] = ((y[va][:, None] - pred) ** 2).mean(axis=0)
    return errs


grid = np.logspace(np.log10(lam_max_d), np.log10(lam_max_d * 1e-3), 60)
errs_l = cv_lasso_path(Xd_tr, yd_tr, grid)
cv_mean_l = errs_l.mean(axis=0)
cv_se_l = errs_l.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(errs_l.shape[0])
i_min = int(np.argmin(cv_mean_l))
i_1se = int(np.where(cv_mean_l <= cv_mean_l[i_min] + cv_se_l[i_min])[0].min())
lam_min, lam_1se = grid[i_min], grid[i_1se]
w_min = Lasso(alpha=lam_min, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=200000).fit(Zd, yc).coef_
w_1se = Lasso(alpha=lam_1se, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=200000).fit(Zd, yc).coef_
S_min, S_1se = np.flatnonzero(w_min), np.flatnonzero(w_1se)
# refit: ordinary least squares on the support selected at lambda_1se (the "relaxed" or "refitted" lasso)
w_refit = np.zeros(p_d)

print(f"one-SE rule: lambda = {lam_1se:.2f}, CV RMSE = {np.sqrt(cv_mean_l[i_1se]):.2f}, {len(S_1se)} features: {', '.join(feat[j] for j in S_1se)}")
print(f"(CV RMSE of the null model: {np.sqrt(cv_mean_l[0]):.2f}; SE of the CV MSE at the minimum: {cv_se_l[i_min]:.0f})")

def figure_10_7():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1]})
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.fill_between(grid, cv_mean_l - cv_se_l, cv_mean_l + cv_se_l, color=SKY, alpha=0.4)
    ax.plot(grid, cv_mean_l, "o-", color=BLUE, ms=3.5, lw=1.5)
    ax.axvline(lam_min, color=VERMILION, ls="--", lw=1.2, label=rf"minimum: $\lambda={lam_min:.2f}$ ({len(S_min)} features)")
    ax.axvline(lam_1se, color=GREEN, ls="-.", lw=1.2, label=rf"one-SE: $\lambda={lam_1se:.2f}$ ({len(S_1se)} features)")
    ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel=r"penalty $\lambda$ (decreasing to the right)", ylabel="10-fold CV mean squared error", title=r"(a) cross-validation along the lasso path")
    ax.invert_xaxis()
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
    ax = axes[1]
    xs = np.arange(p_d)
    wd = 0.27
    ax.bar(xs - wd, w_ols_d, wd, color=SKY, label="least squares")
    ax.bar(xs, w_1se, wd, color=VERMILION, label=r"lasso, one-SE ($\lambda=%.2f$)" % lam_1se)
    ax.bar(xs + wd, w_refit, wd, color=GREEN, label="refit on the same support")
    ax.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xticks(xs)
    ax.set_xticklabels(feat)
    ax.set(ylabel="standardized coefficient", title="(b) shrinkage and refitting")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_10_7()

The cross-validation curve of Figure 10.7(a) is flat for every λ\lambdaλ below about 1: from the minimum at λ=0.54\lambda=0.54λ=0.54 down to the smallest value of the grid the error changes by less than 1%1\%1%, and the standard error at the minimum (195 in MSE, about 1.7 points of RMSE) is larger than any of these differences. The minimum keeps nine features (all but s2; cross-validated RMSE 55.9, against 78.0 for the null model). The one-standard-error rule chooses λ=6.28\lambda = 6.28λ=6.28, which keeps five (sex, bmi, bp, s3, s5, the same five as the one-SE choice for best-subset selection in Section 10.3.2) at a cross-validated RMSE of 57.6, 1.7 points above the minimum, within one standard error by construction. The table and panel (b) show the effect of the penalty on the coefficients. Least squares gives s1 the weight -44.1 and s2 the weight +24.5, the unstable pair of Section 6.2.4; the lasso at the minimum drops s2 and gives s1 -11.5, and also reverses the sign of s3 (+5.5 in least squares, -8.5 in the lasso), another feature whose least-squares weight was an artefact of the collinearity. At the one-SE value the lasso weights are below those of the refit on the same support by an amount that depends on the feature: 2%2\%2% for bmi, 9%9\%9% for s5, 35%35\%35% for bp, 50%50\%50% for s3 (and 95%95\%95% for sex, which is in the model by a hair: -0.5 against -10.9). This is the shrinkage bias of Section 10.5.6; whether the refit predicts better is checked in Section 10.7.3.

10.7.2 Degrees of freedom of the lasso¶

How many degrees of freedom has a lasso fit? Subset selection of size kkk has more than k+1k+1k+1 (Section 10.3.2); the lasso is a continuous shrinkage, so one may expect it to be different. In the orthonormal case the answer is exact, and simple.

Proposition 10.11 (degrees of freedom in the orthonormal case). Let 1nX⊤X=I\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{I}n1​X⊤X=I, y=μ+ε\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\varepsilony=μ+ε with ε∼N(0,σ2I)\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})ε∼N(0,σ2I). The fitted values of the lasso satisfy

df(λ)=1σ2∑i=1nCov⁡(y^i,yi)=E ∥w^λ∥0,\mathrm{df}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Cov}(\hat y_i, y_i) = \mathbb{E}\,\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambda\rVert_0,df(λ)=σ21​i=1∑n​Cov(y^​i​,yi​)=E∥w^λ​∥0​,
(14)

the expected number of non-zero coefficients (plus one for the intercept, if there is one).

Proof

Since Cov⁡(y^i,yi)=E[(y^i−Ey^i)εi]\operatorname{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i) = \mathbb{E}[(\hat y_i - \mathbb{E}\hat y_i)\varepsilon_i]Cov(y^​i​,yi​)=E[(y^​i​−Ey^​i​)εi​], and y^=Xw^\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{w}}y^​=Xw^, we have ∑iCov⁡(y^i,yi)=E[ε⊤X(w^−Ew^)]=∑jE[(xj⊤ε)(w^j−Ew^j)]\sum_i\operatorname{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i) = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol\varepsilon^\top\mathbf{X}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}-\mathbb{E}\hat{\mathbf{w}})] = \sum_j\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\varepsilon)(\hat w_j-\mathbb{E}\hat w_j)]∑i​Cov(y^​i​,yi​)=E[ε⊤X(w^−Ew^)]=∑j​E[(xj⊤​ε)(w^j​−Ew^j​)]. Let Zj=w^jOLS=1nxj⊤y∼N(mj,σ2/n)Z_j = \hat w_j^{\mathrm{OLS}} = \frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(m_j,\sigma^2/n)Zj​=w^jOLS​=n1​xj⊤​y∼N(mj​,σ2/n); then xj⊤ε=n(Zj−mj)\mathbf{x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\varepsilon = n(Z_j-m_j)xj⊤​ε=n(Zj​−mj​) and w^j=Sλ(Zj)\hat w_j = S_\lambda(Z_j)w^j​=Sλ​(Zj​), so the jjj-th term is n E[(Zj−mj)Sλ(Zj)]n\,\mathbb{E}[(Z_j-m_j)S_\lambda(Z_j)]nE[(Zj​−mj​)Sλ​(Zj​)] (subtracting the constant Ew^j\mathbb{E}\hat w_jEw^j​ changes nothing, since E(Zj−mj)=0\mathbb{E}(Z_j-m_j)=0E(Zj​−mj​)=0). Stein’s lemma states that for Z∼N(m,τ2)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(m,\tau^2)Z∼N(m,τ2) and a weakly differentiable fff, E[(Z−m)f(Z)]=τ2E[f′(Z)]\mathbb{E}[(Z-m)f(Z)] = \tau^2\mathbb{E}[f'(Z)]E[(Z−m)f(Z)]=τ2E[f′(Z)]. With f=Sλf = S_\lambdaf=Sλ​, whose derivative is 1{∣z∣>λ}\mathbb{1}\{\lvert z\rvert>\lambda\}1{∣z∣>λ}, and τ2=σ2/n\tau^2 = \sigma^2/nτ2=σ2/n, the jjj-th term is n⋅σ2n P(∣Zj∣>λ)=σ2 P(w^j≠0)n\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\,\mathbb{P}(\lvert Z_j\rvert>\lambda) = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{P}(\hat w_j\neq0)n⋅nσ2​P(∣Zj​∣>λ)=σ2P(w^j​=0). Summing over jjj and dividing by σ2\sigma^2σ2 gives ∑jP(w^j≠0)=E∥w^∥0\sum_j\mathbb{P}(\hat w_j\ne0) = \mathbb{E}\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert_0∑j​P(w^j​=0)=E∥w^∥0​. □\square□

For general designs the same formula holds (Zou, Hastie and Tibshirani, 2007, along the LARS path; Tibshirani and Taylor, 2012, for a fixed λ\lambdaλ, with the number of non-zeros replaced by the rank of the active columns, which is the same when the columns are in general position): the number of non-zero coefficients is an unbiased estimate of the degrees of freedom of the lasso. The contrast with Section 10.3.2 is the point. Best subset selects with a hard threshold and pays for the search with extra degrees of freedom; the lasso shrinks, and the shrinkage of each selected coefficient exactly compensates for the selection, so that the naive count is right. This is what lets CpC_pCp​ and BIC be used with the lasso (the LassoLarsIC estimator of scikit-learn), without a cross-validation. We check it by Monte Carlo in a simulated world on the real design: the truth is the least-squares fit μ=Zw^OLS\boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf{Z}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathrm{OLS}}μ=Zw^OLS​ of the Diabetes training set, and the noise is Gaussian with the estimated σ^=54.8\hat\sigma = 54.8σ^=54.8 (constructed, as in Section 6.3.3). In each of 3,000 replicates we fit the lasso, and estimate df=∑iCov⁡(y^i,yi)/σ2\mathrm{df} = \sum_i\operatorname{Cov}(\hat y_i, y_i)/\sigma^2df=∑i​Cov(y^​i​,yi​)/σ2 directly from the replicates.

def lasso_df_monte_carlo(lams, n_batches=3, per_batch=1000, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mu_true = Zd @ w_ols_d + yd_tr.mean()
    sigma = np.sqrt(sigma2_hat)
    out = {lam: {"df": [], "nz": []} for lam in lams}
    for _ in range(n_batches):
        E = rng.normal(scale=sigma, size=(per_batch, n_d))
        for lam in lams:
            Yh = np.empty((per_batch, n_d))
            nz = np.empty(per_batch)
            for b in range(per_batch):
                m = Lasso(alpha=lam, tol=1e-8).fit(Zd, mu_true + E[b])          # with an intercept
                Yh[b], nz[b] = m.predict(Zd), (m.coef_ != 0).sum()
            out[lam]["df"].append(np.sum((Yh - Yh.mean(axis=0)) * E) / per_batch / sigma ** 2)
            out[lam]["nz"].append(nz.mean() + 1)                                 # + 1 for the intercept
    return out


lams_mc = [0.1, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0]
t0 = time.time()
mc = lasso_df_monte_carlo(lams_mc)
print(pd.DataFrame({"lambda": lams_mc,
                    "df from the covariances": [np.mean(mc[l]["df"]) for l in lams_mc],
                    "SE (3 batches)": [np.std(mc[l]["df"], ddof=1) / np.sqrt(3) for l in lams_mc],
                    "E[number of non-zeros] + 1": [np.mean(mc[l]["nz"]) for l in lams_mc]}).round(2).to_string(index=False))
print(f"({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")

    0.1                    10.86            0.12                       10.71

    3.0                     7.90            0.11                        7.81

The two columns agree within 0.15 for the six values of λ\lambdaλ (at most 1.3 Monte Carlo standard errors), from 10.9 degrees of freedom at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1λ=0.1 to 2.4 at λ=40\lambda=40λ=40, although the design is far from orthonormal: the expected number of non-zero coefficients, plus one for the intercept, is the degrees of freedom of the lasso. Compare with Section 10.3.2, where the best single feature out of ten had 3.4 degrees of freedom instead of one. The lasso with, on average, 1.3 non-zero coefficients at λ=40\lambda=40λ=40 has 2.3 degrees of freedom, intercept included; the shrinkage of the weights compensates for the choice of the features.

Information criteria therefore give a choice of λ\lambdaλ without refitting. With LassoLarsIC (the criteria use the number of non-zero coefficients as degrees of freedom and the noise variance estimated from the full least-squares fit):

ic_fits = {crit: LassoLarsIC(criterion=crit).fit(Zd, yd_tr) for crit in ["aic", "bic"]}
for crit, m in ic_fits.items():
    print(f"{crit.upper()}: lambda = {m.alpha_:.2f}, {int((m.coef_ != 0).sum())} features: {', '.join(feat[j] for j in np.flatnonzero(m.coef_))}")
AIC: lambda = 0.08, 9 features: age, sex, bmi, bp, s1, s2, s4, s5, s6
BIC: lambda = 2.75, 6 features: sex, bmi, bp, s1, s3, s5

The AIC chooses λ=0.08\lambda=0.08λ=0.08 and nine features (all but s3), the BIC chooses λ=2.75\lambda=2.75λ=2.75 and six (sex, bmi, bp, s1, s3, s5): as for best subsets, the BIC gives the smaller model. The six features of the BIC lasso differ from the six of the BIC best subset (Section 10.3.1) by one, s3 in place of s2, another instance of the interchangeable correlated features.

10.7.3 What does sparsity buy on the Diabetes data?¶

We now compare, on the 111 test patients, the methods of this chapter with least squares and ridge regression, all fitted on the 331 training patients with their tuning done only on the training set. This is the single use of the test set in this chapter. The intervals are bootstrap intervals over the test patients (the predictions are fixed and the patients are resampled; Chapter 6 used the same device).

On the 111 test patients all the methods that use the features, from least squares (53.37) to the lasso with the BIC (52.51), lie within 0.9 points of each other, and their bootstrap intervals, 13 to 15 points wide, overlap almost completely: the test set cannot rank them. What it does show is that sparsity costs nothing on these data: five features (the lasso with the one-SE rule, with or without the refit, and the best subset chosen by cross-validation) predict as well as ten (53.1, 52.6 and 52.6 against 53.4 for least squares), and every one of them is far better than the baseline (74.9). The refit of the one-SE support (52.6) is 0.5 points better than the shrunken lasso on the same support (53.1): the shrinkage bias is real, but small compared with the noise of the estimate. The elastic net chose ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ ratio 0.1, which is almost ridge and keeps all ten features: we come back to it in the next section. A comparison on one split of 111 patients is a weak instrument, as Chapter 5 insisted.

A single split of 111 patients cannot rank methods that differ by less than a point, so we repeat the comparison on 30 random splits of the 442 patients (331 for training, 111 for testing), with the tuning inside each training set (5-fold cross-validation for the lasso, the leave-one-out shortcut for ridge), and compare the lasso with ridge with the corrected resampled ttt-test of Section 5.5.2 (and Exercise 6.6). Each split is analyzed with the linear features and, for Section 10.7.5, with all the quadratic features.

def corrected_ttest(a, b, n_train, n_test):
    """Nadeau-Bengio corrected resampled t-test (Section 5.5.2) for paired losses a and b over J splits."""
    d = np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)
    J = len(d)
    t = d.mean() / np.sqrt((1 / J + n_test / n_train) * d.var(ddof=1))
    return d.mean(), t, 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), J - 1)


def lasso_1se_alpha(m):
    mse = m.mse_path_.mean(axis=1)
    se = m.mse_path_.std(axis=1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(m.mse_path_.shape[1])
    i = mse.argmin()
    return m.alphas_[np.where(mse <= mse[i] + se[i])[0].min()]       # alphas_ is decreasing


def repeated_splits(degree, J=30):
    res = {k: [] for k in ["least squares", "ridge", "lasso CV min", "lasso one-SE", "nz min", "nz 1se"]}
    X_all, y_all = diab.data, diab.target
    for r in range(J):
        Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X_all, y_all, test_size=111, random_state=r)
        if degree > 1:
            pf = PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False)
            Xa, Xb = pf.fit_transform(Xa), pf.transform(Xb)
        sc = StandardScaler().fit(Xa)
        A, B = sc.transform(Xa), sc.transform(Xb)
        res["least squares"].append(np.mean((LinearRegression().fit(A, ya).predict(B) - yb) ** 2))
        res["ridge"].append(np.mean((RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-1, 5, 40)).fit(A, ya).predict(B) - yb) ** 2))
        lc = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=r).fit(A, ya)
        res["lasso CV min"].append(np.mean((lc.predict(B) - yb) ** 2))
        l1 = Lasso(alpha=lasso_1se_alpha(lc)).fit(A, ya)
        res["lasso one-SE"].append(np.mean((l1.predict(B) - yb) ** 2))
        res["nz min"].append((lc.coef_ != 0).sum())
        res["nz 1se"].append((l1.coef_ != 0).sum())
    return res

rs_lin, rs_quad = repeated_splits(1), repeated_splits(2)

for name in ["least squares", "ridge", "lasso CV min", "lasso one-SE"]:

    rows.append({"method (linear features)": name, "test RMSE (mean of 30 splits)": np.sqrt(np.mean(rs_lin[name])),
                 "difference of MSE vs ridge": d, "corrected t": t, "p-value": pv})

print(f"features selected on average: CV minimum {np.mean(rs_lin['nz min']):.1f}, one-SE {np.mean(rs_lin['nz 1se']):.1f} (of 10)")

Over 30 splits the mean test RMSE is 54.9 for least squares, 55.0 for ridge and 54.9 for the lasso at its cross-validation minimum, which keeps 8.2 of the ten features on average; none of the differences from ridge is significant (corrected p=0.54p=0.54p=0.54 and 0.67). The one-standard-error rule keeps only 4.6 features on average and costs about 1.3 points of RMSE (56.3; the difference in MSE with ridge is 134, corrected p=0.18p = 0.18p=0.18): a more parsimonious model at a price that the data do not resolve. The reason that nothing is gained is in Theorem 6.1: with n=331n=331n=331 and p=10p=10p=10 the excess error of least squares is σ2p/n≈91\sigma^2p/n\approx 91σ2p/n≈91, about 3%3\%3% of the mean squared error (≈3,000\approx3{,}000≈3,000), and there is little variance to remove by shrinking or selecting. The benefit of sparsity appears when ppp is large compared with nnn.

10.7.4 Many irrelevant features: the logarithm of ppp¶

The strongest argument for the lasso is not the Diabetes data, which have ten features, but the situation of Section 4.7.2: many features, most of them useless. We repeat that experiment for linear models. The data are the Diabetes patients with mmm columns of independent Gaussian noise appended (the same device as in Section 4.7.2: the 10 real features are untouched and the noise is, by construction, irrelevant). For each mmm we draw 20 random training sets of n=100n = 100n=100 patients, test on the other 342, and compare the baseline (mean of the training targets), least squares (when p<np<np<n), ridge regression (leave-one-out choice of λ\lambdaλ) and the lasso (5-fold cross-validation), with the features standardized on each training set.

def noise_columns_experiment(ms, n_train=100, reps=20):
    X_all, y_all = diab.data, diab.target
    rows = []
    for m_noise in ms:
        acc = {"baseline": [], "least squares": [], "ridge": [], "lasso": [], "noise features selected": [], "features selected": []}
        for r in range(reps):
            rng = np.random.default_rng(1000 + r)
            Z_all = np.hstack([X_all, rng.normal(size=(len(X_all), m_noise))]) if m_noise else X_all
            Za, Zb, ya, yb = train_test_split(Z_all, y_all, train_size=n_train, random_state=r)
            sc = StandardScaler().fit(Za)
            A, B = sc.transform(Za), sc.transform(Zb)
            rmse = lambda pred: np.sqrt(np.mean((pred - yb) ** 2))
            acc["baseline"].append(rmse(ya.mean()))
            if Z_all.shape[1] < n_train - 5:
                acc["least squares"].append(rmse(LinearRegression().fit(A, ya).predict(B)))
            acc["ridge"].append(rmse(RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-2, 4, 40)).fit(A, ya).predict(B)))
            lc = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=r).fit(A, ya)
            acc["lasso"].append(rmse(lc.predict(B)))
            acc["features selected"].append((lc.coef_ != 0).sum())
            acc["noise features selected"].append((lc.coef_[10:] != 0).sum())
        rows.append({"noise columns m": m_noise, "p": 10 + m_noise, **{k: (np.mean(v) if v else np.nan) for k, v in acc.items()}})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


t0 = time.time()
noise_table2 = noise_columns_experiment([0, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000])

figure_10_8()

Figure 10.8(a) gives the picture that the theory of the next paragraphs explains. Least squares fails first: with 30 noise columns (p=40p=40p=40 for n=100n=100n=100) its RMSE is 70.3, and it cannot be computed beyond p≈np\approx np≈n. Ridge degrades steadily with the number of useless columns, from 56.4 to 72.8 at m=1000m=1000m=1000, which is 80%80\%80% of the way to the baseline of 76.8: ridge spreads the weight over every feature and pays σ2/n\sigma^2/nσ2/n for each. The lasso goes from 56.9 to 60.6, 19%19\%19% of the way: its error grows very slowly with mmm (the two curves cross between m=0m=0m=0 and m=10m=10m=10). Panel (b) shows how: out of 1,000 noise columns the lasso keeps, on average, 11 (1.1%1.1\%1.1%), while the number of real features that it keeps falls from 7.0 to 3.4, because with 100 patients the weak real features can no longer be told from the noise. The lasso pays for its ignorance of the support by losing the weakest real features, not by fitting the noise.

The behavior of the lasso is explained by a bound in which the number of features appears only through its logarithm. We assume that the columns are normalized, ∥xj∥2=n\lVert\mathbf{x}_j\rVert^2 = n∥xj​∥2=n, and that y=Xw∗+ε\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}^\ast + \boldsymbol\varepsilony=Xw∗+ε with ε∼N(0,σ2I)\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})ε∼N(0,σ2I). Nothing is assumed about the sparsity of w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ or the correlation of the features: the bound involves only ∥w∗∥1\lVert\mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert_1∥w∗∥1​.

Read (10.7) as a statement about the price of features: the dimension enters through ln⁡p\sqrt{\ln p}lnp​, so multiplying the number of useless features by 10 adds a constant to the bound. Compare the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​-ball Rademacher complexity of Exercise 3.9, which has the same 2ln⁡2p\sqrt{2\ln 2p}2ln2p​ factor, while the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ complexity and the error of ridge or least squares grow with the dimension itself. The bound is “slow” because it decreases as 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ instead of sln⁡p/ns\ln p/nslnp/n; the fast rate needs conditions on the correlation of the features (the restricted eigenvalue condition of Bickel, Ritov and Tsybakov, 2009, in the further reading), which the bound above does not need.

10.7.5 Sparse nonlinear features¶

Section 6.7 found that adding all the quadratic features to ridge regression on Diabetes did not help. A sparse model can pick the few interactions that matter out of the 65=10+10⋅11/265 = 10 + 10\cdot11/265=10+10⋅11/2 features of degree at most two, so the lasso is the natural way to try the idea again. We use the 30 splits of the previous experiment, with the quadratic features computed on each training set.

Least squares on the 65 quadratic features is clearly worse than linear ridge (62.6 against 55.0, corrected p=0.04p = 0.04p=0.04), ridge on the quadratic features loses a little (56.5, p=0.22p=0.22p=0.22), and the lasso at its minimum recovers the linear performance exactly (54.9, with 17.3 of the 65 features selected on average): it beats the quadratic ridge by 177 in MSE (corrected p=0.063p=0.063p=0.063, suggestive but not significant). So the sparse quadratic model removes the damage of the extra features, but it does not improve on the linear model, which is the conclusion of Section 6.7. The single 331/111331/111331/111 split would have told another story: the quadratic lasso reached a test RMSE of 50.8 against 53.0 for the linear lasso on the same patients, a gain of 2.2 points that disappears across 30 splits (54.92 against 54.94): that split was lucky, the lesson of Chapter 5 again. The largest coefficients are those of the linear model (bmi, s5, bp, s3) followed by sex^2, age sex, bmi^2 and s6^2. One detail is a small lesson of its own: sex takes only two values in this data set, so sex^2 is an affine function of sex and the two columns are perfectly correlated; the lasso kept sex^2 and not sex, an arbitrary choice among identical columns, which is the subject of Exercise 10.3 and of the next section.

10.8 Correlated features and the elastic net¶

The lasso has a weakness that the previous sections have already shown twice. On the Diabetes path (Figure 10.5) the correlated features s1, s2 and s3 leave and re-enter the model, and in the quadratic experiment the lasso kept sex^2 and dropped sex, although the two columns are identical. When several features carry the same information the lasso keeps one of them, and which one depends on small perturbations of the data: it is a coin toss. If the features are only similar, as the three serum measurements are, the toss can change from one sample to the next, and the list of selected features is not reproducible. A remedy that keeps the sparsity and removes the toss was proposed by Zou and Hastie (2005): add a ridge penalty.

Definition 10.3 (elastic net)

For λ1>0\lambda_1>0λ1​>0 and λ2≥0\lambda_2\ge0λ2​≥0, the elastic net estimator minimizes

Fλ1,λ2(w)=12n∥y−Zw∥2+λ1∥w∥1+λ22∥w∥22.(10.8)F_{\lambda_1,\lambda_2}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + \lambda_1\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2^2. \tag{10.8}Fλ1​,λ2​​(w)=2n1​∥y−Zw∥2+λ1​∥w∥1​+2λ2​​∥w∥22​.(10.8)
(17)

In scikit-learn, ElasticNet(alpha, l1_ratio) has λ1=alpha⋅l1_ratio\lambda_1 = \text{alpha}\cdot\text{l1\_ratio}λ1​=alpha⋅l1_ratio and λ2=alpha (1−l1_ratio)\lambda_2 = \text{alpha}\,(1-\text{l1\_ratio})λ2​=alpha(1−l1_ratio).

The objective is strictly convex for λ2>0\lambda_2>0λ2​>0, so the solution is unique even when p>np>np>n or when columns are repeated, and it keeps the zeros of the lasso, because the penalty is still non-differentiable at wj=0w_j=0wj​=0. Everything we learned about the lasso carries over, thanks to a trick.

Proposition 10.13 (the elastic net is a lasso on augmented data)

Let Z~=[Znλ2 Ip]∈R(n+p)×p\tilde{\mathbf{Z}} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{Z}\\ \sqrt{n\lambda_2}\,\mathbf{I}_p\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+p)\times p}Z~=[Znλ2​​Ip​​]∈R(n+p)×p and y~=[y0]\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{y}\\ \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}y~​=[y0​]. Then Fλ1,λ2(w)=12n∥y~−Z~w∥2+λ1∥w∥1F_{\lambda_1,\lambda_2}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1{2n}\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{y}}-\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2+\lambda_1\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1Fλ1​,λ2​​(w)=2n1​∥y~​−Z~w∥2+λ1​∥w∥1​ for every w\mathbf{w}w: the elastic net on (Z,y)(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{y})(Z,y) is a lasso problem on (n+p)(n+p)(n+p) examples, whose design has rank ppp whatever Z\mathbf{Z}Z is.

Proof. ∥y~−Z~w∥2=∥y−Zw∥2+nλ2∥w∥2\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{y}}-\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + n\lambda_2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2∥y~​−Z~w∥2=∥y−Zw∥2+nλ2​∥w∥2; divide by 2n2n2n. □\square□

The proposition says that every solver of Section 10.6 solves the elastic net, that the coordinate update is wj←Sλ1(⋅)/(1+λ2)w_j\leftarrow S_{\lambda_1}(\cdot)/(1+\lambda_2)wj​←Sλ1​​(⋅)/(1+λ2​) (the extra term adds λ2\lambda_2λ2​ to the curvature 1n∥zj∥2=1\frac1n\lVert\mathbf{z}_j\rVert^2=1n1​∥zj​∥2=1), and, by the rank statement, that the solution is unique. The next cell checks the identity on the Diabetes training set and then repeats the column of bmi.

lam1, lam2 = 2.0, 1.0
en_fit = ElasticNet(alpha=lam1 + lam2, l1_ratio=lam1 / (lam1 + lam2), fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=200000).fit(Zd, yc)
Z_aug = np.vstack([Zd, np.sqrt(n_d * lam2) * np.eye(p_d)])
y_aug = np.r_[yc, np.zeros(p_d)]
# scikit-learn divides the squared error by 2 * (number of rows): n + p here, not n
las_aug = Lasso(alpha=lam1 * n_d / (n_d + p_d), fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=200000).fit(Z_aug, y_aug)
print(f"elastic net on (Z, y) vs lasso on the augmented data: max |difference of the weights| = {np.abs(en_fit.coef_ - las_aug.coef_).max():.1e}")
print(f"non-zero weights of the elastic net (lambda1={lam1}, lambda2={lam2}): {int((en_fit.coef_ != 0).sum())} of {p_d}")

# Repeated column: the data term depends only on the sum of the two weights.
Z_dup = np.column_stack([Zd, Zd[:, 2]])          # the last column is a copy of bmi (column 2)
rows = []
for name, l1, l2 in [("lasso", 6.0, 0.0), ("elastic net", 6.0, 6.0)]:
    m = ElasticNet(alpha=l1 + l2, l1_ratio=l1 / (l1 + l2), fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=200000).fit(Z_dup, yc)
    rows.append({"method": name, "weight of bmi": m.coef_[2], "weight of its copy": m.coef_[10], "sum": m.coef_[2] + m.coef_[10]})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))
elastic net on (Z, y) vs lasso on the augmented data: max |difference of the weights| = 2.2e-15
non-zero weights of the elastic net (lambda1=2.0, lambda2=1.0): 9 of 10
     method  weight of bmi  weight of its copy    sum
      lasso         24.390               0.417 24.807
elastic net          4.266               4.266  8.531

The identity holds to 2⋅10−152\cdot10^{-15}2⋅10−15: the elastic net on (Z,y)(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{y})(Z,y) and the lasso on the augmented data return the same vector (nine of the ten features are kept for λ1=2\lambda_1=2λ1​=2, λ2=1\lambda_2=1λ2​=1). With the copy of bmi appended, the data term depends only on the sum of the two weights, so the lasso is indifferent to how the sum is split between the two columns: any split with the same sign has the same objective, and the solver returns one of them, 24.4 and 0.4 (another algorithm, or the columns in another order, would return another). The elastic net returns the equal split, 4.27 and 4.27, which by strict convexity is the unique minimizer. The sum is smaller than that of the lasso (8.5 against 24.8) because the second penalty, with λ2=6\lambda_2=6λ2​=6 large compared with the curvature 1 of the data term, also shrinks.

10.8.1 The grouping effect¶

The repeated column is the extreme case. The theorem says that the equal split is not an accident of exact copies: it degrades gracefully with the correlation.

Theorem 10.14 (grouping effect; Zou and Hastie, 2005)

Let the columns of Z\mathbf{Z}Z be standardized, 1n∥zj∥2=1\frac1n\lVert\mathbf{z}_j\rVert^2=1n1​∥zj​∥2=1, the response centered, λ2>0\lambda_2>0λ2​>0, and let w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^ minimize (10.8). Write ρij=1nzi⊤zj\rho_{ij} = \frac1n\mathbf{z}_i^\top\mathbf{z}_jρij​=n1​zi⊤​zj​. If w^iw^j>0\hat w_i\hat w_j>0w^i​w^j​>0 (both weights non-zero, with the same sign), then

∣w^i−w^j∣ ≤ ∥y∥n λ22(1−ρij).(10.9)\lvert\hat w_i-\hat w_j\rvert\ \le\ \frac{\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert}{\sqrt{n}\,\lambda_2}\sqrt{2(1-\rho_{ij})}. \tag{10.9}∣w^i​−w^j​∣ ≤ n​λ2​∥y∥​2(1−ρij​)​.(10.9)
(18)

In particular two identical columns (ρij=1\rho_{ij}=1ρij​=1) that are both selected receive the same weight.

Proof

Let r=y−Zw^\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{Z}\hat{\mathbf{w}}r=y−Zw^. The optimality condition of Theorem 10.7 with the extra term λ2wj\lambda_2 w_jλ2​wj​ says that, for a coordinate with w^j≠0\hat w_j\ne0w^j​=0, −1nzj⊤r+λ1sign⁡(w^j)+λ2w^j=0-\frac1n\mathbf{z}_j^\top\mathbf{r}+\lambda_1\operatorname{sign}(\hat w_j)+\lambda_2\hat w_j=0−n1​zj⊤​r+λ1​sign(w^j​)+λ2​w^j​=0. Write it for iii and jjj and subtract: since the signs are equal, the terms in λ1\lambda_1λ1​ cancel and λ2(w^i−w^j)=1n(zi−zj)⊤r\lambda_2(\hat w_i-\hat w_j)=\frac1n(\mathbf{z}_i-\mathbf{z}_j)^\top\mathbf{r}λ2​(w^i​−w^j​)=n1​(zi​−zj​)⊤r. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, ∣w^i−w^j∣≤1nλ2∥zi−zj∥∥r∥\lvert\hat w_i-\hat w_j\rvert\le\frac1{n\lambda_2}\lVert\mathbf{z}_i-\mathbf{z}_j\rVert\lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert∣w^i​−w^j​∣≤nλ2​1​∥zi​−zj​∥∥r∥, and ∥zi−zj∥2=2n(1−ρij)\lVert\mathbf{z}_i-\mathbf{z}_j\rVert^2 = 2n(1-\rho_{ij})∥zi​−zj​∥2=2n(1−ρij​). Finally F(w^)≤F(0)F(\hat{\mathbf{w}})\le F(\mathbf{0})F(w^)≤F(0) gives 12n∥r∥2≤12n∥y∥2\frac1{2n}\lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert^2\le\frac1{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^22n1​∥r∥2≤2n1​∥y∥2, so ∥r∥≤∥y∥\lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert\le\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert∥r∥≤∥y∥. Combining the three facts gives (10.9). □\square□

The bound is proportional to 1/λ21/\lambda_21/λ2​ (no ridge, no grouping: the lasso is the case λ2=0\lambda_2=0λ2​=0, where the bound is vacuous) and to 1−ρij\sqrt{1-\rho_{ij}}1−ρij​​. It is not tight, as the experiment will show, but it is a guarantee that holds for every sample. The experiment below is a constructed example, flagged as such: we add to the Diabetes training features a twin of bmi, equal to bmi plus Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of a tenth of that of bmi (correlation 0.996), and ask whether the methods split the weight of bmi consistently between the two when the training set is resampled. We draw 200 bootstrap samples of the 331 training patients, and on each we standardize, fit the lasso (λ1=1\lambda_1=1λ1​=1) and the elastic net (λ1=1\lambda_1=1λ1​=1, λ2=1\lambda_2=1λ2​=1) and record the weights of the two columns.

tw_rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
twin = Xd_tr[:, 2] + 0.1 * Xd_tr[:, 2].std() * tw_rng.normal(size=n_d)
XT = np.column_stack([Xd_tr, twin])                    # 11 columns: the ten features and the twin of bmi
print(f"correlation between bmi and its twin: {np.corrcoef(XT[:, 2], XT[:, 10])[0, 1]:.4f}")


def fit_en(X, y, l1, l2):
    """Standardize, center y, fit the elastic net (l2 = 0 is the lasso); return weights and the quantities of Theorem 10.14."""
    Zs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
    yy = y - y.mean()
    m = ElasticNet(alpha=l1 + l2, l1_ratio=l1 / (l1 + l2), fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-10, max_iter=100000).fit(Zs, yy)
    rho = Zs[:, 2] @ Zs[:, 10] / len(yy)
    return m.coef_, rho, np.linalg.norm(yy) / np.sqrt(len(yy))


tw_B = 200
tw_idx = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 1).integers(0, n_d, size=(tw_B, n_d))
tw = {}
for name, l1, l2 in [("lasso", 1.0, 0.0), ("elastic net", 1.0, 1.0)]:
    out = [fit_en(XT[ix], yd_tr[ix], l1, l2) for ix in tw_idx]
    W = np.array([o[0] for o in out])
    bound = np.array([o[2] * np.sqrt(2 * (1 - o[1])) / l2 if l2 > 0 else np.inf for o in out])
    tw[name] = {"W": W, "bound": bound, "l2": l2}

rows = []
for name, d in tw.items():
    W = d["W"]
    both = (W[:, 2] * W[:, 10] > 0)
    gap = np.abs(W[:, 2] - W[:, 10])
    rows.append({"method": name,
                 "mean w(bmi)": W[:, 2].mean(), "mean w(twin)": W[:, 10].mean(),
                 "sd w(bmi)": W[:, 2].std(), "sd of the sum": (W[:, 2] + W[:, 10]).std(),
                 "only one of the two non-zero": np.mean((W[:, [2, 10]] != 0).sum(axis=1) == 1),
                 "max gap |w(bmi) - w(twin)|": gap.max(),
                 "replicates with both non-zero, same sign": int(both.sum()),
                 "bound (10.9) holds in all of them": bool(np.all(gap[both] <= d["bound"][both] + 1e-9)) if d["l2"] > 0 else "no bound"})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).T.to_string(header=False))
print(f"median value of the bound (10.9) for the elastic net: {np.median(tw['elastic net']['bound']):.2f}")
correlation between bmi and its twin: 0.9957

method                                       lasso  elastic net
mean w(bmi)                                 12.659       10.392
mean w(twin)                                13.406       10.386
sd w(bmi)                                   11.627        1.151
sd of the sum                                4.093          2.3
only one of the two non-zero                  0.67          0.0
max gap |w(bmi) - w(twin)|                  37.784        0.814
replicates with both non-zero, same sign        66          200
bound (10.9) holds in all of them         no bound         True

The lasso knows the total weight but not how to divide it. The mean weights of the two columns are similar (12.7 and 13.4) but each of them has a standard deviation of about 12, the standard deviation of their sum is only 4.1, and in 67%67\%67% of the samples exactly one of the two columns is non-zero (both were non-zero, with the same sign, in only 66 of the 200 samples); the scatter plot of Figure 10.9(a) shows the lasso’s samples lying on the two axes, with gaps as large as 38. The elastic net gives both columns a non-zero weight in all 200 samples, the two weights are almost equal (the largest gap is 0.8) and each has a standard deviation of 1.2. The bound (10.9) holds in all 200 samples, with a median value of 7.2, nine times the largest gap observed: it is a guarantee, not a prediction of the size of the effect.

10.8.2 Stability of the selected set¶

Does the elastic net also select a more reproducible set? We measure it on the ten real Diabetes features, without the twin. For each of 100 bootstrap samples we fit the model, record the selected set, and measure the agreement of two sets AAA and BBB by the Jaccard index ∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣\lvert A\cap B\rvert/\lvert A\cup B\rvert∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣, averaged over 2,000 random pairs of bootstrap samples. A larger model is trivially more stable (the full set of ten features always agrees with itself), so the comparison is meaningful only at equal model size: we trace the mean Jaccard index against the mean number of selected features as the penalty varies, for the lasso and for the elastic net with λ1=λ2\lambda_1=\lambda_2λ1​=λ2​ (l1_ratio=0.5).

def stability_curve(alphas, l1_ratio, B=100):
    """Mean model size and mean pairwise Jaccard index of the selected sets over B bootstrap samples, for each alpha."""
    idx_b = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 2).integers(0, n_d, size=(B, n_d))
    pairs = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 3).integers(0, B, size=(2000, 2))
    pairs = pairs[pairs[:, 0] != pairs[:, 1]]
    out = []
    for a in alphas:
        sel = np.zeros((B, p_d), bool)
        for b, ix in enumerate(idx_b):
            Zs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xd_tr[ix])
            sel[b] = ElasticNet(alpha=a, l1_ratio=l1_ratio, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-8, max_iter=50000).fit(Zs, yd_tr[ix] - yd_tr[ix].mean()).coef_ != 0
        inter = (sel[pairs[:, 0]] & sel[pairs[:, 1]]).sum(axis=1)
        union = (sel[pairs[:, 0]] | sel[pairs[:, 1]]).sum(axis=1)
        out.append((sel.sum(axis=1).mean(), np.mean(np.where(union > 0, inter / np.maximum(union, 1), 1.0)), sel.mean(axis=0)))
    return out


stab_lasso = stability_curve(np.logspace(-0.5, 1.7, 12), 1.0)
stab_en = stability_curve(np.logspace(0.0, 1.9, 12), 0.5)
rows = []
for name, st in [("lasso", stab_lasso), ("elastic net, l1_ratio 0.5", stab_en)]:
    for size, jac, freq in st[::2]:
        rows.append({"method": name, "mean model size": size, "mean Jaccard index": jac})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))
for name, st in [("lasso", stab_lasso), ("elastic net", stab_en)]:
    k = int(np.argmin([abs(s[0] - 7.0) for s in st]))
    print(f"{name}, the setting with mean size nearest to 7 ({st[k][0]:.2f}): selection frequency of " + ", ".join(f"{f}: {q:.2f}" for f, q in zip(feat, st[k][2])))

def figure_10_9():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.4))
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.scatter(tw["lasso"]["W"][:, 2], tw["lasso"]["W"][:, 10], s=18, color=VERMILION, alpha=0.6, label="lasso")
    ax.scatter(tw["elastic net"]["W"][:, 2], tw["elastic net"]["W"][:, 10], s=18, color=BLUE, alpha=0.6, label="elastic net")
    lim = [-3, max(tw["lasso"]["W"][:, [2, 10]].max(), 20) * 1.05]
    ax.plot(lim, lim, color="gray", lw=0.8)
    ax.set(xlabel="weight of `bmi`", ylabel="weight of its twin", title="(a) 200 bootstrap samples, two nearly identical columns", xlim=lim, ylim=lim)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.plot([s[0] for s in stab_lasso], [s[1] for s in stab_lasso], "o-", color=VERMILION, lw=2, label="lasso")
    ax.plot([s[0] for s in stab_en], [s[1] for s in stab_en], "s-", color=BLUE, lw=2, label=r"elastic net, $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$")
    ax.set(xlabel="mean number of selected features", ylabel="mean Jaccard index of two bootstrap selections", title="(b) stability of the selected set", ylim=(0.3, 1.02))
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_10_9()

Figure 10.9(b) shows that at the same model size the elastic net is more reproducible than the lasso, but not uniformly and not by much. For models of between five and eight features on average, the mean Jaccard index of the lasso falls to 0.71 to 0.74 and that of the elastic net stays between 0.85 and 0.87; at the two ends (nearly the full model, or two or three features) the curves are close. The frequencies at the setting with seven features say what the difference is. The lasso always keeps bmi, bp, s3 and s5 and nearly always sex (0.93), and tosses a coin among age, s1, s2, s4 and s6 (frequencies 0.16 to 0.46). The elastic net keeps bmi, bp, s3, s4, s5 and s6 in every sample, age in 69%69\%69% and never sex: a reproducible set, but a different one from the lasso’s. Stability measures how well the procedure agrees with itself on resampled data, not whether the selected set is the true one. The figure is one data set and 100 resamples, and the wiggles of the curves show its noise: we take from it the direction of the effect, not its size. On Diabetes the cross-validated elastic net of Section 10.7.3 chose an ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ ratio of 0.1, nearly ridge, and kept all ten features: the prediction does not need the selection.

10.9 Sparse classification¶

Everything in this chapter carries over to classification by changing the loss. The ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​-penalized logistic regression minimizes the average logistic loss plus the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm of the weights, with the intercept left free:

min⁡b,w  1n∑i=1n[ln⁡ ⁣(1+eb+zi⊤w)−yi (b+zi⊤w)]+λ∥w∥1,yi∈{0,1}.(10.10)\min_{b,\mathbf{w}}\ \ \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\Big[\ln\!\big(1+e^{b+\mathbf{z}_i^\top\mathbf{w}}\big)-y_i\,(b+\mathbf{z}_i^\top\mathbf{w})\Big]+\lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1,\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\}. \tag{10.10}b,wmin​  n1​i=1∑n​[ln(1+eb+zi⊤​w)−yi​(b+zi⊤​w)]+λ∥w∥1​,yi​∈{0,1}.(10.10)
(19)

The objective is convex but not quadratic, so the soft-threshold of Proposition 10.6 is not exact, but proximal gradient works unchanged (the gradient of the loss is Lipschitz, Section 6.5) and so does coordinate descent with a quadratic approximation of the loss at each step. In scikit-learn the problem is LogisticRegression(l1_ratio=1, solver="saga", C=C) with λ=1/(nC)\lambda = 1/(nC)λ=1/(nC) (the liblinear solver would also penalize the intercept, and we avoid it). The optimality condition at w=0\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}w=0 gives the analogue of Theorem 10.7.

Proposition 10.15 (the smallest penalty that gives the zero model)

Let the columns of Z\mathbf{Z}Z be standardized. The minimizer of (10.10) has w^=0\hat{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{0}w^=0 if and only if λ≥λmax⁡=1n∥Z⊤(y−yˉ1)∥∞\lambda\ge\lambda_{\max} = \frac1n\lVert\mathbf{Z}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})\rVert_\inftyλ≥λmax​=n1​∥Z⊤(y−yˉ​1)∥∞​, and then b^=ln⁡yˉ1−yˉ\hat b=\ln\frac{\bar y}{1-\bar y}b^=ln1−yˉ​yˉ​​.

Proof. The derivative of the loss with respect to bbb is 1n∑i(σ(b+zi⊤w)−yi)\frac1n\sum_i(\sigma(b+\mathbf{z}_i^\top\mathbf{w})-y_i)n1​∑i​(σ(b+zi⊤​w)−yi​); at w=0\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}w=0 it vanishes if and only if σ(b)=yˉ\sigma(b)=\bar yσ(b)=yˉ​, which gives b^\hat bb^. The derivative with respect to wjw_jwj​ at that point is 1n∑i(yˉ−yi)zij=−1nzj⊤(y−yˉ1)\frac1n\sum_i(\bar y-y_i)z_{ij} = -\frac1n\mathbf{z}_j^\top(\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})n1​∑i​(yˉ​−yi​)zij​=−n1​zj⊤​(y−yˉ​1), and by the optimality condition for a convex function plus λ∥⋅∥1\lambda\lVert\cdot\rVert_1λ∥⋅∥1​ (the argument of Theorem 10.7), w=0\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}w=0 is optimal if and only if ∣1nzj⊤(y−yˉ1)∣≤λ\lvert\frac1n\mathbf{z}_j^\top(\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})\rvert\le\lambda∣n1​zj⊤​(y−yˉ​1)∣≤λ for all jjj. □\square□

We use the Breast Cancer data with the stratified 426/143426/143426/143 split of Chapters 6, 8 and 9, malignant =1=1=1, standardized with the training statistics.

bc = load_breast_cancer()
bc_y_all = 1 - bc.target                                        # malignant = 1, as in Chapter 6
bc_Xtr, bc_Xte, bc_ytr, bc_yte = train_test_split(bc.data, bc_y_all, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=bc_y_all)
bc_sc = StandardScaler().fit(bc_Xtr)
bc_Ztr, bc_Zte = bc_sc.transform(bc_Xtr), bc_sc.transform(bc_Xte)
bc_n, bc_p = bc_Ztr.shape
print(f"{bc_n} training and {len(bc_yte)} test examples, {bc_p} features, {bc_ytr.sum()} malignant in the training set")


def make_logit(C, l1_ratio, tol, warm=False):
    """l1 penalty (l1_ratio = 1): saga; l2 penalty (l1_ratio = 0): the default lbfgs solver, much faster for this penalty."""
    if l1_ratio == 0:
        return LogisticRegression(C=C, tol=tol, max_iter=100000, warm_start=warm)
    return LogisticRegression(l1_ratio=l1_ratio, C=C, solver="saga", max_iter=100000, tol=tol, warm_start=warm)


def logit(Z, y, C, l1_ratio, tol=1e-8):
    return make_logit(C, l1_ratio, tol).fit(Z, y)


def logit_path(Z, y, Cs, l1_ratio, tol=1e-6, max_iter=3000):
    """Solutions along an increasing grid of C, each warm-started from the previous one. The cap on the iterations of saga only matters for
    the weakest penalties (near-separable data), far to the right of the cross-validation minimum."""
    m = make_logit(Cs[0], l1_ratio, tol, warm=True).set_params(max_iter=max_iter)
    W, b = [], []
    for C in Cs:
        m.set_params(C=C).fit(Z, y)
        W.append(m.coef_[0].copy()); b.append(m.intercept_[0])
    return np.array(W), np.array(b)


def path_log_loss(Z, y, W, b):
    """Log loss of every solution of a path on (Z, y): returns one value per row of W."""
    z = Z @ W.T + b
    return np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, z) - y[:, None] * z, axis=0)


lam_max_lg = np.max(np.abs(bc_Ztr.T @ (bc_ytr - bc_ytr.mean()))) / bc_n
C_max = 1 / (bc_n * lam_max_lg)
grad0 = np.abs(bc_Ztr.T @ (bc_ytr - bc_ytr.mean())) / bc_n          # |gradient of the loss at w = 0|, one value per feature
top2 = np.argsort(-grad0)[:2]
first = ", ".join(f"{bc.feature_names[j]} ({grad0[j]:.4f})" for j in top2)
for f in [0.98, 1.0005]:
    m = logit(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr, f * C_max, 1.0, tol=1e-12)
    print(f"C = {f:.2f} * C_max ({f * C_max:.4f}): {int((m.coef_ != 0).sum())} non-zero weight(s)" + (f" ({bc.feature_names[np.flatnonzero(m.coef_[0])[0]]})" if (m.coef_ != 0).any() else ""))
print(f"lambda_max = {lam_max_lg:.4f}, C_max = 1/(n lambda_max) = {C_max:.4f}; logit of the malignant fraction: {np.log(bc_ytr.mean() / (1 - bc_ytr.mean())):+.3f}; the two largest values of |gradient| (the first features to enter): {first}")
426 training and 143 test examples, 30 features, 159 malignant in the training set
C = 0.98 * C_max (0.0061): 0 non-zero weight(s)

C = 1.00 * C_max (0.0062): 1 non-zero weight(s) (worst concave points)
lambda_max = 0.3774, C_max = 1/(n lambda_max) = 0.0062; logit of the malignant fraction: -0.518; the two largest values of |gradient| (the first features to enter): worst concave points (0.3774), worst perimeter (0.3769)

At 0.98 Cmax⁡0.98\,C_{\max}0.98Cmax​ the solver returns the zero vector, and at 1.0005 Cmax⁡1.0005\,C_{\max}1.0005Cmax​ a single non-zero weight, that of worst concave points, the feature with the largest absolute gradient (0.3774), as the proposition says. The runner-up, worst perimeter, is only 0.1%0.1\%0.1% behind (0.3769), so a factor of 1.02 would already have admitted it: the first feature to enter is decided by a hair when features are this correlated. (We do not print the intercept of the solver for the zero model: saga stops as soon as the weights stop changing, so its intercept is only accurate to about 0.01, whereas the proposition gives it exactly, -0.518.)

We now choose CCC by 10-fold cross-validated log loss on the training set, for the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ and the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty, with the one-standard-error rule for the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ model, and evaluate each choice once on the 143 test patients.

bc_grid = np.logspace(-2.2, 0.4, 14)
bc_skf = StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
bc_cv = {}
t0 = time.time()
for pen, l1r in [("l1", 1.0), ("l2", 0.0)]:
    L = np.zeros((len(bc_grid), 10))
    for f, (tr, va) in enumerate(bc_skf.split(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr)):
        W_, b_ = logit_path(bc_Ztr[tr], bc_ytr[tr], bc_grid, l1r)
        L[:, f] = path_log_loss(bc_Ztr[va], bc_ytr[va], W_, b_)
    bc_cv[pen] = (L.mean(axis=1), L.std(axis=1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(10))
print(f"[cross-validation: {time.time() - t0:.0f} s]")

bc_choice = {}
k_min = int(np.argmin(bc_cv["l1"][0]))
thr = bc_cv["l1"][0][k_min] + bc_cv["l1"][1][k_min]
bc_choice["l1, CV minimum"] = ("l1", 1.0, bc_grid[k_min])
bc_choice["l1, one-SE"] = ("l1", 1.0, bc_grid[np.flatnonzero(bc_cv["l1"][0] <= thr)[0]])
bc_choice["l2, CV minimum"] = ("l2", 0.0, bc_grid[int(np.argmin(bc_cv["l2"][0]))])
rows, bc_models = [], {}
for name, (pen, l1r, C) in bc_choice.items():
    m = logit(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr, C, l1r, tol=1e-10)
    bc_models[name] = m
    pr = m.predict_proba(bc_Zte)[:, 1]
    rows.append({"model": name, "C": C, "non-zero weights": int((m.coef_ != 0).sum()), "CV log loss": bc_cv[pen][0][list(bc_grid).index(C)],
                 "test log loss": log_loss(bc_yte, pr), "test errors (of 143)": int((m.predict(bc_Zte) != bc_yte).sum())})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))
m1 = bc_models["l1, one-SE"]
print("one-SE model:", ", ".join(f"{bc.feature_names[j]} ({m1.coef_[0, j]:+.2f})" for j in np.argsort(-np.abs(m1.coef_[0]))[: int((m1.coef_ != 0).sum())]))

def figure_10_10():
    path_C = np.logspace(-2.2, 0.4, 40)
    W, _ = logit_path(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr, path_C, 1.0)
    w1 = bc_models["l1, one-SE"].coef_[0]
    sel = np.argsort(-np.abs(w1))[:7]                              # the seven largest weights of the one-SE model are drawn in color
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.4))
    ax = axes[0]
    for j in range(bc_p):
        if j not in sel:
            ax.semilogx(path_C, W[:, j], color="gray", lw=0.7, alpha=0.45)
    colors = [BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN, VERMILION, SKY, PURPLE, "black"]
    for c, j in zip(colors, sel):
        ax.semilogx(path_C, W[:, j], color=c, lw=2, label=bc.feature_names[j])
    ax.axvline(bc_choice["l1, one-SE"][2], color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.axvline(bc_choice["l1, CV minimum"][2], color="black", ls=":", lw=1)
    ax.set(xlabel="C (larger C: weaker penalty)", ylabel="weight", title=r"(a) $\ell_1$-logistic path (dashed: one-SE; dotted: CV min.)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper left", ncol=1)
    ax = axes[1]
    for pen, c, lab in [("l1", VERMILION, r"$\ell_1$"), ("l2", BLUE, r"$\ell_2$ (ridge)")]:
        mu, se = bc_cv[pen]
        ax.semilogx(bc_grid, mu, color=c, lw=2, label=lab)
        ax.fill_between(bc_grid, mu - se, mu + se, color=c, alpha=0.2)
    ax.set(xlabel="C", ylabel="10-fold CV log loss", title="(b) cross-validated log loss", ylim=(0, 0.45))
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_10_10()

Panel (b) of Figure 10.10 shows that the two penalties are not competitors on prediction: with a strong penalty the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ model is worse (it has few features and shrinks the rest to zero: at the left end of the grid the model is empty), and from C≈0.6C\approx 0.6C≈0.6 on the two curves coincide, with minima of 0.0828 (ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​) and 0.0824 (ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​), both at C=1C=1C=1. On the 143 test patients the three models make 4, 3 and 5 errors (log loss 0.073, 0.072 and 0.078), and the difference between 3 and 5 errors is within the noise (the standard error of an accuracy near 97%97\%97% on 143 patients is 1.4 points, about two patients, Section 5.2.2). What sparsity bought here is modest in size: the one-SE model keeps 12 of the 30 features, not the five that one might hope for, because the 30 features are three versions (mean, standard error, worst value) of the same 10 measurements, and several of them are nearly collinear; the largest weights are those of worst radius, radius error, worst texture and mean concave points. Panel (a) shows once more the non-monotone path of the lasso: the weight of worst radius, the largest at the one-SE value (+3.03), rises, then falls to zero at the right end of the grid, while other features take over.

10.9.1 When p>np>np>n: the weights leave the row space¶

Chapter 9 proved that for the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty the solution is a combination of the training examples (Theorem 9.4): w^=∑iαizi\hat{\mathbf{w}}=\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbf{z}_iw^=∑i​αi​zi​ lies in the row space of Z\mathbf{Z}Z, a subspace of dimension at most nnn, so that when p>np>np>n the weights along the directions orthogonal to every training example are exactly zero. The ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ penalty is not a function of the length of w\mathbf{w}w, but of its coordinates, and the theorem does not apply: the sparse solution has its zeros along the coordinate axes, and these do not respect the row space. We verify it on a real problem of the right shape, the Digits data restricted to the digits 3 and 8 (images of 8×88\times88×8 pixels, so p=64p=64p=64), with a random subset of n=40n=40n=40 training images, and then look at the weights on a larger training set.

dg = load_digits()
dg_mask = (dg.target == 3) | (dg.target == 8)
dg_X, dg_y = dg.data[dg_mask], (dg.target[dg_mask] == 8).astype(int)
dg_Xtr, dg_Xte, dg_ytr, dg_yte = train_test_split(dg_X, dg_y, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=dg_y)
dg_sc = StandardScaler().fit(dg_Xtr)
live = dg_Xtr.std(axis=0) > 0                                        # a few border pixels are constant (always zero)
dg_Ztr, dg_Zte = dg_sc.transform(dg_Xtr), dg_sc.transform(dg_Xte)
dg_Ztr[:, ~live], dg_Zte[:, ~live] = 0, 0
print(f"{len(dg_ytr)} training and {len(dg_yte)} test images of the digits 3 and 8; {int(live.sum())} of the 64 pixels are not constant")

sub = np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(len(dg_ytr), 40, replace=False)
Zs, ys = dg_Ztr[sub], dg_ytr[sub]
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(Zs.T)                                     # orthonormal basis of the row space of Zs (rank <= 40)
print(f"n = 40, rank of the data matrix = {np.linalg.matrix_rank(Zs)}, p = 64")
rows = []
for name, l1r, C in [("l2", 0.0, 0.1), ("l1", 1.0, 0.1), ("l1", 1.0, 0.3)]:
    m = logit(Zs, ys, C, l1r, tol=1e-12)
    w = m.coef_[0]
    rows.append({"penalty": name, "C": C, "non-zero weights": int((w != 0).sum()),
                 "relative distance of w to the row space": np.linalg.norm(w - Q @ (Q.T @ w)) / np.linalg.norm(w)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2e}" if isinstance(v, float) and v < 1e-2 else f"{v:.3f}"))
267 training and 90 test images of the digits 3 and 8; 54 of the 64 pixels are not constant
n = 40, rank of the data matrix = 40, p = 64
penalty     C  non-zero weights  relative distance of w to the row space
     l2 0.100                54                                 5.13e-16
     l1 0.100                 3                                    0.434
     l1 0.300                 7                                    0.427

For the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty the weights are in the row space to machine precision (relative distance 4⋅10−164\cdot10^{-16}4⋅10−16), as Theorem 9.4 says; they use all the 54 pixels that are not constant in this data set (the other ten are zero for every training image). The ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ solutions are sparse (3 and 7 pixels out of 64), and about 43%43\%43% of their length lies outside the row space: they are not combinations of the 40 images, and no dual problem in 40 variables describes them. This is not a defect of the penalty: it is what lets it choose coordinates. It means that the kernel trick does not apply to an ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​-penalized model, which has to be solved in the ppp weights, and that its cost grows with ppp and not with nnn.

On the full training set of 267 images, chosen by cross-validation, the two penalties give the weight maps of Figure 10.11.

dg_skf = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
dg_grid = np.logspace(-2.5, 1.5, 17)
dg_cv = {}
for pen, l1r in [("l1", 1.0), ("l2", 0.0)]:
    L = np.zeros((len(dg_grid), 5))
    for f, (tr, va) in enumerate(dg_skf.split(dg_Ztr, dg_ytr)):
        W_, b_ = logit_path(dg_Ztr[tr], dg_ytr[tr], dg_grid, l1r)
        L[:, f] = path_log_loss(dg_Ztr[va], dg_ytr[va], W_, b_)
    dg_cv[pen] = L.mean(axis=1)
print(pd.DataFrame({"C": dg_grid, "l1 CV log loss": dg_cv["l1"], "l2 CV log loss": dg_cv["l2"]}).iloc[::2].round(4).to_string(index=False))
dg_models, rows = {}, []
for pen, l1r in [("l2", 0.0), ("l1", 1.0)]:
    C = dg_grid[int(np.argmin(dg_cv[pen]))]
    m = logit(dg_Ztr, dg_ytr, C, l1r, tol=1e-10)
    dg_models[pen] = m
    rows.append({"penalty": pen, "C chosen by CV": C, "pixels with non-zero weight": int((m.coef_ != 0).sum()),
                 "test log loss": log_loss(dg_yte, m.predict_proba(dg_Zte)[:, 1]), "test errors": f"{int((m.predict(dg_Zte) != dg_yte).sum())} of {len(dg_yte)}"})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))

On these data the cross-validated log loss falls with CCC up to the end of the grid for both penalties (0.0253 for ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ and 0.0172 for ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ at C=31.6C=31.6C=31.6): the digits 3 and 8 are almost linearly separable in their 54 informative pixels, so the best penalty is the weakest one that we tried (we stop there: beyond it the curves are nearly flat and saga becomes very slow), and the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ curve is below the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ curve at every CCC. The ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ model uses all 54 pixels and makes no error on the 90 test images (log loss 0.014); the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ model uses 21 of them, makes 2 errors (log loss 0.039), and its weight map in Figure 10.11(b) is a thinned-out version of the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ map, with nonzero weights in the same central region where the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ weights are largest. Two errors against none, on 90 images, is not a difference that the data can confirm; what is clear is that the sparse model costs something in log loss here, while giving a map of 21 pixels that a person can inspect.

10.10 Filters, wrappers and embedded methods¶

The methods of this chapter are embedded: the selection happens while the model is fitted, as a by-product of the penalty. Two other families are in common use, and they are worth placing next to it.

familyhow it selectsexamplescostsees interactions?
filterscores each feature on its own, by a statistic computed once, and keeps the best kkkcorrelation, ANOVA FFF-statistic, mutual informationone pass over the featuresno: each feature is judged alone
wrappersearches over subsets, fitting a model to evaluate eachforward and backward selection, recursive feature elimination (RFE)many fits of the modelyes, through the model
embeddedthe fit of the model itself sets some weights to zerolasso, elastic net, ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ logistic regression, treesone path of fitsyes, through the model

The weakness of a filter on correlated features is easy to predict: if three features measure nearly the same thing and each of them is correlated with the response, the filter keeps all three and wastes the budget of kkk features. The Breast Cancer data have exactly this structure (radius, perimeter and area of a nucleus are different transformations of its size, measured as a mean, as a standard error and as the worst value in the image). We compare the three families on the 426 training patients with 10-fold cross-validation, with the selection inside every fold (the topic of the next section): an FFF-statistic filter, RFE with an ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ logistic model (a wrapper), and the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​-penalized logistic regression, whose number of features is varied through CCC.

bc_names = bc.feature_names
corr_tr = np.corrcoef(bc_Ztr.T)


def redundancy(S):
    """Largest absolute correlation between two selected features."""
    S = list(S)
    return max(abs(corr_tr[i, j]) for i, j in itertools.combinations(S, 2)) if len(S) > 1 else 0.0


k_sel = 5
filt = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=k_sel).fit(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr)
wrap = RFE(LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000), n_features_to_select=k_sel, step=1).fit(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr)
emb_C = next(C for C in np.logspace(-2.2, -0.3, 200) if (logit(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr, C, 1.0, tol=1e-6).coef_ != 0).sum() >= k_sel)
emb = logit(bc_Ztr, bc_ytr, emb_C, 1.0, tol=1e-10)
chosen = {"filter (F-statistic)": np.flatnonzero(filt.get_support()), "wrapper (RFE)": np.flatnonzero(wrap.get_support()),
          "embedded (l1 logistic)": np.argsort(-np.abs(emb.coef_[0]))[:k_sel]}
for name, S in chosen.items():
    print(f"{name:<24} {', '.join(bc_names[j] for j in S)}")
    print(f"{'':<24} largest correlation between two of the five: {redundancy(S):.3f}")

embedded (l1 logistic)   worst radius, worst concave points, mean concave points, worst texture, worst symmetry
                         largest correlation between two of the five: 0.908

for k in ks:
    for name, sel in [("filter", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=k)), ("wrapper (RFE)", RFE(LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000), n_features_to_select=k, step=1))]:
        pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), sel, LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))
        rows.append({"method": name, "features": k, "CV log loss": -cross_val_score(pipe, bc_Xtr, bc_ytr, cv=cv10, scoring="neg_log_loss").mean(),
                     "CV accuracy": cross_val_score(pipe, bc_Xtr, bc_ytr, cv=cv10, scoring="accuracy").mean()})
for C in np.logspace(-1.9, -0.3, 10):          # embedded: the l1 model selects, an l2 model is fitted on what it selects
    sel_l1 = SelectFromModel(LogisticRegression(l1_ratio=1, C=C, solver="saga", max_iter=20000, tol=1e-6))
    pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), sel_l1, LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))
    ll, ac, nz = [], [], []
    for tr, va in cv10.split(bc_Xtr, bc_ytr):
        pipe.fit(bc_Xtr[tr], bc_ytr[tr])
        ll.append(log_loss(bc_ytr[va], pipe.predict_proba(bc_Xtr[va])[:, 1])); ac.append(pipe.score(bc_Xtr[va], bc_ytr[va])); nz.append(int(pipe[1].get_support().sum()))
    rows.append({"method": "embedded (l1)", "features": float(np.mean(nz)), "CV log loss": np.mean(ll), "CV accuracy": np.mean(ac)})
sel_cmp = pd.DataFrame(rows)

The five features chosen by the filter include three that measure the size of the nucleus (mean perimeter, worst radius, worst perimeter), with a correlation of 0.994 between two of them: the filter scores each feature alone, and all the size features score high. RFE and the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ model pick more varied sets (the largest correlation inside the five is 0.983 and 0.908): the elimination and the penalty both look at a feature given the others. The cross-validated log loss of Figure 10.12, with the selection inside each fold, shows the cost. With five features the filter has 0.145 and RFE 0.109; the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ selection followed by an ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ fit has 0.110 with 5.1 features on average. The filter stays near 0.14 from five to ten features, improves slightly at fifteen (0.132) and reaches the level of the others only at twenty (0.081), when the less redundant features have finally entered. The gap of about 0.035 is about three standard errors of the cross-validation estimate (≈0.01\approx0.01≈0.01, Figure 10.10(b)). The difference between RFE and the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ selection is within the noise, and the three families agree when the budget is large: the cost of a filter is paid when features are few and redundant. These are one data set and one 10-fold split, and the cost of RFE (here 30 refits per fold at most) is the reason that it is not used when ppp is in the thousands, while a single ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ path is.

10.11 Selection belongs inside the loop¶

Chapter 2 showed that preprocessing fitted on all the data leaks information from the validation fold, and Section 4.7.2 that SelectKBest must be a step of the pipeline. Feature selection is the strongest case of this rule, because it uses the labels. A selector that has seen the label of an example has been fitted with it, and any estimate of the error of the final model on that example is optimistic. The experiment below makes the effect as large as possible, in a world in which the right answer is known: real features, shuffled labels (flagged in the data note of Section 10.1), so that by construction no feature carries information about the label and every honest method must have an expected accuracy of 50%50\%50%. We take 40 images of the digits 3 and 8 and append 500 columns of Gaussian noise to their 64 pixels, shuffle the labels, keep the 5 features with the largest FFF-statistic, and estimate the accuracy of a logistic regression on them by 5-fold cross-validation, in two ways: selecting the five features once on all 40 examples (the leak), or inside each training fold (the pipeline). The experiment is repeated 200 times with different images, noise and shuffles.

def leak_experiment(reps=200, n=40, k=5, extra=500):
    leaky, honest = [], []
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="Features .* are constant")       # some border pixels are constant in a sample of 40 images
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="invalid value encountered in divide")
    for r in range(reps):
        rg = np.random.default_rng(1000 + r)
        ix = rg.choice(len(dg_X), n, replace=False)
        Xl = np.column_stack([dg_X[ix], rg.normal(size=(n, extra))])
        yl = rg.permutation(np.r_[np.zeros(n // 2, int), np.ones(n // 2, int)])            # independent of the features
        cvl = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=r)
        Xsel = StandardScaler().fit_transform(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=k).fit(Xl, yl).transform(Xl))   # selection sees every label
        leaky.append(cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), Xsel, yl, cv=cvl).mean())
        pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(f_classif, k=k), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
        honest.append(cross_val_score(pipe, Xl, yl, cv=cvl).mean())
    return np.array(leaky), np.array(honest)


t0 = time.time()
leaky, honest = leak_experiment()
print(f"[{time.time() - t0:.0f} s]")
print(pd.DataFrame({"selection": ["on all the data (leak)", "inside each fold (pipeline)"],
                    "mean CV accuracy": [leaky.mean(), honest.mean()], "sd": [leaky.std(), honest.std()],
                    "5th to 95th percentile": [f"{np.percentile(leaky, 5):.2f} to {np.percentile(leaky, 95):.2f}", f"{np.percentile(honest, 5):.2f} to {np.percentile(honest, 95):.2f}"]}).round(3).to_string(index=False))
print(f"repetitions in which the leaky estimate is above 0.70: {np.mean(leaky > 0.70):.0%}; of the honest estimate: {np.mean(honest > 0.70):.0%}")
[6 s]
                  selection  mean CV accuracy    sd 5th to 95th percentile
     on all the data (leak)             0.814 0.055           0.72 to 0.90
inside each fold (pipeline)             0.497 0.103           0.35 to 0.68
repetitions in which the leaky estimate is above 0.70: 97%; of the honest estimate: 4%

The result is as large as the theory allows. Selecting the features on all the data first makes a classifier with no information whatsoever about the label look like one that is right four times in five: the mean cross-validated accuracy is 0.81 (the 5th to 95th percentiles are 0.72 and 0.90), and in 97%97\%97% of the repetitions it exceeds 0.70. Selecting inside the folds gives 0.497, the right answer, with a wide spread (0.35 to 0.68: 40 examples do not allow a precise estimate) in which only 4%4\%4% of the repetitions exceed 0.70. The mechanism is the one of Section 2.7: the five features that the selector kept are those that, by chance, separate the 40 labels best, and they separate them in the validation folds too because the validation labels took part in the choice. With 564 candidate features and 40 examples there are always five that look informative.

The same mistake has a second form, which concerns statistical tests and not predictions. After the data have chosen the feature that looks best, the usual ppp-value of that feature is not a ppp-value any more: it is the smallest of several, and it is small more often than 5%5\%5% of the time even when nothing is there. We measure it on the ten real Diabetes features with shuffled responses, so that the null hypothesis holds for every feature. In each of 5,000 shuffles we pick the feature with the largest ∣t∣\lvert t\rvert∣t∣ and report its ordinary ppp-value, computed (i) on the same data (the naive procedure), or (ii) on a disjoint half of the patients that did not take part in the choice (data splitting).

ps_rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 5)
Xall = StandardScaler().fit_transform(diab.data)
n_all = len(Xall)


def best_feature_p(X, y):
    r = (X - X.mean(0)).T @ (y - y.mean()) / (len(y) * X.std(0) * y.std())
    t = r * np.sqrt((len(y) - 2) / (1 - r ** 2))
    j = int(np.argmax(np.abs(t)))
    return j, 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t[j]), len(y) - 2)


naive, split = [], []
for _ in range(5000):
    yp = ps_rng.permutation(diab.target)
    naive.append(best_feature_p(Xall, yp)[1])
    h = ps_rng.permutation(n_all)
    j, _ = best_feature_p(Xall[h[:n_all // 2]], yp[h[:n_all // 2]])
    xj = Xall[h[n_all // 2:], j]; yj = yp[h[n_all // 2:]]
    r = np.corrcoef(xj, yj)[0, 1]
    split.append(2 * stats.t.sf(abs(r * np.sqrt((len(yj) - 2) / (1 - r ** 2))), len(yj) - 2))
naive, split = np.array(naive), np.array(split)
print(pd.DataFrame({"p-value of the selected feature": ["naive (same data)", "data splitting (selection on one half, test on the other)"],
                    "fraction of shuffles with p < 0.05": [np.mean(naive < 0.05), np.mean(split < 0.05)],
                    "mean p-value": [naive.mean(), split.mean()]}).round(3).to_string(index=False))


def figure_10_13():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.2))
    ax = axes[0]
    bins = np.linspace(0.2, 1.0, 33)
    ax.hist(leaky, bins=bins, color=VERMILION, alpha=0.75, label="selection on all the data (leak)")
    ax.hist(honest, bins=bins, color=BLUE, alpha=0.75, label="selection inside each fold")
    ax.axvline(0.5, color="black", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set(xlabel="5-fold CV accuracy (true accuracy: 0.5)", ylabel="repetitions (of 200)", title="(a) accuracy of a classifier on shuffled labels")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    ax = axes[1]
    b = np.linspace(0, 1, 21)
    ax.hist(naive, bins=b, color=VERMILION, alpha=0.75, label="naive p-value of the selected feature")
    ax.hist(split, bins=b, histtype="step", color=BLUE, lw=2.2, label="data splitting")
    ax.axhline(5000 / 20, color="black", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set(xlabel="p-value", ylabel="shuffles (of 5,000)", title="(b) a valid p-value is uniform on [0, 1]")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
